content.text: THE MASTER SAHIB EDUCATIONAL SERIESCLASS VII ENGLISH — UNIT 2SOCIAL ETIQUETTES AND MANNERS(Complete Solved Textbook Exercises)
■  UNIT 2: SOCIAL ETIQUETTES AND MANNERS (SOLVED TEXTBOOK EXERCISES)
► 2.1 Reading Comprehension: Problems and Solutions (Letters to Big Brother)
Understanding good manners, courteous social conduct, and mutual respect:
Pre-Reading Q1. What do we mean when we say that someone has good manners?

Ans: Good manners mean treating others with kindness, respect, consideration, and patience. It involves speaking politely, listening attentively, greeting elders warmly, using magic words like 'please' and 'thank you', and respecting social rules.
Pre-Reading Q2. What do we mean when we say that someone has bad manners?

Ans: Bad manners refer to rude, selfish, or inconsiderate behaviour such as talking harshly, interrupting conversations, chewing food noisily, mocking others, or ignoring the comfort of elderly and special people.
Pre-Reading Q3. What will happen if everyone behaves in a good manner?
Ans: If everyone behaves courteously, society becomes peaceful, orderly, and cooperative. Mutual trust, friendship, and happiness flourish, while unnecessary friction and anger disappear.
Pre-Reading Q4. What will happen if everyone behaves in a bad manner?
Ans: If people behave rudely and selfishly, social harmony collapses. Arguments, resentment, chaos, hurt feelings, and hostility will destroy relationships in families, schools, and communities.
Explanation: All five letter writers study in Class VI, VII, and IX, which belong to the secondary school section.
Grandparents consider him ill-mannered though he does not speak harshly.
Asked to give up his bus seat for others despite paying full fare.
Often scolded at lunch and dinner times for poor table manners.
Argues frequently with his best friend Abid over different viewpoints.
Feels inferior because she has a darker skin complexion than peers.
having a physical or mental disability
make fun of someone in an unkind way
rebuked or spoken angrily to for doing wrong
rude; not having good social manners
continuing to exist for a very long time
natural color and appearance of skin
feeling lower in status, rank or quality
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 3: TRUE OR FALSE STATEMENTS
Zain's grandparents disliked him and never visited his home.
False — They loved him dearly but expected more warmth and attentiveness from him.
Ahsan should feel honoured when selected to give comfort to an elderly person on the bus.
True — Offering your seat to those in greater need is a noble civic deed and a blessing.
Fahad was advised to chew his food with his mouth wide open.
False — Big Brother advised him to chew with his mouth strictly closed and never speak with food inside.
Good friends should always force each other to agree on every single opinion.
False — True friendship requires respecting diversity of opinion and letting friends win arguments sometimes.
A person's worth and likeability are determined by skin complexion and facial beauty.
False — Worth is determined entirely by cleanliness, polite speech, character, and generous conduct.
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 4: BIG BROTHER'S SOLUTIONS & ADVICE SUMMARY
Welcome them with a bright smile, carry their bags, sit and listen patiently to their stories, and treat their irritation with gentle kindness.
Giving up a seat for the elderly or weak is a badge of honour, not weakness. Ignore teasing peers and take pride in serving others.
Allow elders to take food first; chew with closed mouth; do not speak while eating; help serve and clean the dining table.
Accept that differences in opinions are natural in society. Listen to his views before speaking, and sometimes let him win arguments.
Physical appearance does not define character. Maintain impeccable hygiene, well-combed hair, clean clothes, and an affectionate, helpful personality.
Sentence: Word: 'harsh'Sentence: Our Holy Prophet (PBUH) taught us never to use harsh words when speaking to elders or servants.
Sentence: Word: 'valuable tips'Sentence: The career counsellor shared valuable tips on how to prepare systematically for board exams.
Sentence: Word: 'mock'Sentence: It is disgraceful and cruel to mock people who have physical deformities or speak with a stammer.
Sentence: Word: 'impolite'Sentence: It is extremely impolite to check mobile phone messages while someone is talking directly to you.
Sentence: Word: 'lasting'Sentence: Mutual trust, honesty, and forgiveness are the cornerstones of a lasting friendship.
Q: Why did Zain's grandparents think he was ill-mannered even though he never misbehaved?

Ans: Zain's grandparents felt he was ill-mannered because older people crave emotional warmth, attention, and companionship. While Zain never spoke harshly, he was passive, did not greet them warmly, failed to offer assistance with their luggage, and did not sit down to listen to their conversation.
Q: Why should young students willingly give up their seats on public transport for elderly people?

Ans: Students have young, energetic bodies and greater physical endurance. Elderly citizens, pregnant women, and handicapped persons experience severe pain and risk injury from sudden bus brakes. Offering one's seat is a practical demonstration of civic nobility, empathy, and Islamic teachings of respecting elders.
Q: List four fundamental dining etiquettes that everyone should practice at home and at social events.

Ans: Four fundamental table manners are: (1) Allow elders and guests to take food first, (2) Chew food quietly with the mouth closed and never talk with food in the mouth, (3) Never slurp drinks or burp aloud at the table, and (4) Assist politely in serving dishes and clearing the table after meals.
Q: How does learning to accept diverse viewpoints strengthen personal friendships?

Ans: Human beings are raised with different backgrounds, personalities, and perspectives. When we accept diverse views rather than demanding total conformity, we foster mutual respect and intellectual maturity. By listening patiently and occasionally conceding arguments, friends build unbreakable trust and emotional security.
Q: What truly makes a human being likeable and respected in society according to Big Brother?

Ans: According to Big Brother, neither fair skin, tall height, nor expensive garments make an individual respectable. True likeability springs from high personal hygiene, neat clothing, clean shoes, polite speech, a cheerful smile, forgiveness, and a sincere willingness to help others without arrogance.
► 2.2 Speaking: Giving Reasons for Opinions and Actions
• Speaking Focus: Giving Logical Reasons for Actions
Useful conversational phrases for expressing polite opinions and backing them with sound logical reasons:
• 'In my opinion...', • 'I firmly believe that...', • 'The main reason for this is...', • 'From my perspective...'

• Situation 1: Giving up a seat on a crowded busStudent A: 'Why did you stand up and offer your seat to that old gentleman?'Student B: 'In my opinion, it is our civic and moral duty. The reason is that his frail legs could not handle the sudden jolts of the bus, and helping him brought peace to my heart.'

• Situation 2: Respecting dining etiquettes at family dinnersStudent A: 'Why does your mother insist on chewing with your mouth closed?'Student B: 'I believe she is completely right because chewing openly looks repulsive and can spray food particles, which is extremely disrespectful to everyone sitting at the table.'

• Situation 3: Handling disagreements among classmatesStudent A: 'Why didn't you fight back when Tariq disagreed with your cricket strategy?'Student B: 'The reason is that every teammate has a right to express his point of view. A lasting friendship is far more precious than winning a petty argument.'
► 2.3 Language Practice: Articles (A, An, The) & Reflexive Pronouns
• Grammar Rules: Indefinite (A, An) & Definite (The) Articles
• 'A': Used before singular countable nouns beginning with a consonant sound (e.g., a boy, a seat, a polite child).
• 'An': Used before singular countable nouns beginning with a vowel sound (e.g., an apple, an elder, an honest boy [silent h], an hour).
• 'The': Definite article used for specific things, unique objects (the sun, the sky), names of rivers/seas (the Indus), and things mentioned a second time.
■ EXERCISE 1: ARTICLES FILL IN THE BLANKS
Item: (1) Ahsan is an honest boy who always pays his bus fare.
Item: (2) Zain welcomed his grandfather with a warm smile.
Item: (3) Fahad sat at the head of the family dinner table.
Item: (4) Abid has a unique perspective on every topic.
Item: (5) Sania realized that an attractive character is better than fair skin.
Item: (6) We must cross the road carefully at the zebra crossing.
Item: (7) Giving your seat to an elderly person is a noble deed.
Item: (8) He waited for an hour outside the principal's office.
I prepared the entire presentation on civic manners all by myself.
You should take pride in yourself when performing good deeds.
Ahsan himself offered his seat to the frail passenger.
Sania taught herself to ignore negative comments and stay confident.
The problem of urban littering will not solve itself without citizen effort.
We organized the neighbourhood cleaning drive ourselves.
Boys, you must behave yourselves while visiting the museum.

Sentence (i): Original: Zain looked at (Zain's reflection) in the mirror.Solved: Zain looked at himself in the mirror.
Sentence (ii): Original: I promised (my own mind) never to speak harshly to elders.Solved: I promised myself never to speak harshly to elders.
Sentence (iii): Original: The children cleaned the dining table (without any outside help).Solved: The children cleaned the dining table themselves.
Sentence (iv): Original: Sania, you should believe in (your own abilities).Solved: Sania, you should believe in yourself.
Sentence (v): Original: We must prepare (our group) for the debate competition.Solved: We must prepare ourselves for the debate competition.
Sentence (vi): Original: My sister bought a novel for (her own reading).Solved: My sister bought a novel for herself.
► 2.4 Writing: Short Informal Letters on Etiquette and Friendship
• Key Structural Features of Short Informal Letters
• Sender's Address: House / Flat number, Street, City (Top right corner).
• Body Paragraphs: Friendly tone, clear purpose of writing, and warm personal closing.
• Complimentary Close & Signature: 'Your sincere friend, / Yours affectionately,' followed by name.
■ MODEL LETTER 1: APOLOGIZING TO A FRIEND AFTER AN ARGUMENT
Model Informal Letter 1: Apologizing to a Friend After a Heated Argument

Assalamo Alaikum! I am writing this letter with a humble and sincere heart to apologize for my behaviour yesterday during our discussion after school. I spoke too loudly and insisted stubbornly that only my strategy for the science model was correct.

After reflecting on our talk, I realized that I failed to listen to your valuable viewpoint. True friendship is built on mutual respect and patience, not on winning every disagreement. You are my closest and most caring friend, and our bond is infinitely more important to me than any petty argument. Please forgive my impatience. Let us meet tomorrow at the library so we can combine both of our ideas for the project.
Please convey my deepest regards to your respected parents and love to little Hamza.
■ MODEL LETTER 2: ADVISING A YOUNGER COUSIN ON RESPECTING GRANDPARENTS
Model Informal Letter 2: Advising a Younger Cousin on Respecting Grandparents

I hope this letter finds you in the best of health and spirits. Aunt Amna told me that Dada Jan and Dadi Jan are coming to stay at your home for the winter vacations. I am writing to share some friendly tips on how you can make their stay wonderful.

Grandparents love us immensely, but because of old age and weakness, they sometimes get tired and easily irritated. When they arrive, welcome them at the door with a bright smile, carry their bags, and serve them water before they even ask. Dedicate at least half an hour every evening to sit beside them, listen attentively to their childhood memories, and press their tired feet if they permit. These small gestures of courtesy bring countless blessings and immense joy to their hearts.
I am sure you will prove to be an exemplary, loving grandson. Write back soon and let me know how you are doing in school.
► 2.5 Study Skills: Cloze Passage Technique for Language Mastery
A cloze passage tests your reading comprehension and grammar awareness by removing words at regular intervals. Fill each blank with the most appropriate word from the provided bank:
Word Bank: respect, manners, peaceful, listen, polite, elderly, cleanliness, character

Good (1) ________ are the foundation of a civilized and dignified society. When we treat others with courtesy and (2) ________, we create an atmosphere where everyone feels valued and safe. A truly cultured person does not judge others by their wealth or appearance, but by the nobility of their (3) ________. In daily life, we should always speak in a (4) ________ tone, offer our seats to the (5) ________ and disabled, and (6) ________ patiently when others speak. Moreover, maintaining personal (7) ________ and keeping our surroundings tidy reflect our moral values. Practising these golden habits ensures a happy, cooperative, and (8) ________ community.
(1) manners, (2) respect, (3) character, (4) polite, (5) elderly, (6) listen, (7) cleanliness, (8) peaceful
► 2.6 Fun Time: Humorous Solutions to Everyday Etiquette Dilemmas
• Dilemma 1: What to do when your aunt serves you burnt, rock-hard biscuits?
Humorous Solution: Smile sweetly, tell her they are the crunchiest cookies you have ever tasted in your life, and quietly dip them in hot tea for 5 minutes until they become edible!
• Dilemma 2: What to do when someone snores loudly next to you in the mosque or van?
Humorous Solution: Don't poke them angrily! Softly start reciting SubhanAllah aloud in a melodious voice so they wake up gently, thinking it's the morning prayer call!
• Dilemma 3: What to do when your stomach grumbles loudly during a pin-drop silent classroom exam?
Humorous Solution: Instantly press your stomach, look down sternly at your tummy, and whisper loud enough for the teacher to hear: 'Be quiet in there! We are taking an exam!'

content.text: THE MASTER SAHIB EDUCATIONAL SERIESCLASS VII ENGLISH — UNIT 3AWARENESS OF CRISIS, ACCIDENTS, AND NATURAL CALAMITIES(Complete Solved Textbook Exercises)
■  UNIT 3: AWARENESS OF CRISIS, ACCIDENTS, AND NATURAL CALAMITIES (SOLVED TEXTBOOK EXERCISES)
► 3.1 Reading Comprehension: Learning to Live in a Critical Situation (Flood Survival)
Understanding monsoon disasters, safety measures, and flood resilience:
Pre-Reading Q1. What happens when it rains a lot in the monsoon season?

Ans: During heavy, incessant monsoon downpours, rivers and canals overflow their banks, low-lying villages are submerged under flash floods, mud houses collapse, standing crops are ruined, and road communications are severed.
Pre-Reading Q2. What kinds of problems do people face during natural calamities?

Ans: People face loss of shelter, displacement, shortage of food and potable drinking water, power cuts, outbreak of waterborne epidemics (cholera, gastroenteritis), and tragic loss of loved ones and livestock.
Pre-Reading Q3. Does somebody help them or do they help themselves?

Ans: Initially, neighbours and local community members help one another to reach higher ground. Subsequently, the Pakistan Armed Forces, rescue agencies (Rescue 1122, Edhi Foundation), and government relief camps provide emergency boats, rations, tents, and medical aid.
Pre-Reading Q4. What would you do if you found yourself in such an emergency situation?

Ans: I would remain calm, switch off the main electrical power, pack vital family documents and emergency medicines in waterproof bags, evacuate promptly to elevated safe zones, and actively assist women, young children, and elderly people.
■ WHILE-READING EXERCISE 1: ZUBAIR'S SURVIVAL ON THE FLOATING LOG
Q: What object had Zubair and his mother held onto during the terrifying flood night, and where did it take him?

Ans: Zubair and his mother had desperately clung to a floating tree log throughout the wild night. The water currents carried the log until it gently bumped against a small, elevated tract of land at dawn where Zubair survived, though his mother was tragically swept away.
flowing quickly and in large quantities
held on very tightly to something
unable to feel anything due to cold or shock
walked with difficulty through water or mud
extremely tired and devoid of energy
not bright; having very little light
temporary shelter providing food and aid to victims
careful to avoid potential dangers or mistakes
sudden, disastrous events causing great damage
move away from a dangerous place to a safer area
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 3: TRUE OR FALSE STATEMENTS
Zubair was rescued by his neighbours on a motorcycle.
False — He was rescued by brave Pakistan Army soldiers sailing in an emergency boat.
The soldiers brought Zubair to an emergency relief camp that provided shelter and food.
True — The camp offered shelter, cooked food, and life-saving medicines to hundreds of displaced victims.
Zubair gave up completely and decided never to help anyone else in his life.
False — He channelled his personal tragedy into community service by educating others on flood safety.
Walking in just six inches of rapidly flowing water can cause an adult to fall.
True — As little as 6 inches (15 cm) of rushing floodwater carries tremendous force and can knock a person down.
Zubair and the young relief worker wrote flood safety rules on large white bedsheets.
True — They displayed clear safety instructions on large bedsheets to instruct and train camp residents.
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 4: FLOOD SAFETY RULES CATEGORIZATION TABLE

• Regularly monitor weather forecasts and emergency radio warnings.• Prepare a grab-bag containing non-perishable food, flashlight, first aid, and documents.• Disconnect all electrical appliances and switch off the main gas/power supplies.• Move immediately to higher ground upon official evacuation notices.

• Never walk, swim, or drive through moving floodwaters.• Use a sturdy stick to test the firmness and depth of ground before taking steps.• Hold the hands of young children, frail elders, and special persons.• Stay far away from fallen power cables and sagging electric poles.

• Return home only after local disaster management authorities declare the area safe.• Boil all drinking water vigorously to prevent cholera, typhoid, and diarrhea.• Inspect walls and roof beams for structural cracks before stepping inside.• Clean and disinfect all mud-soaked surfaces to eliminate germs and reptiles.
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 5: CHRONOLOGICAL SEQUENCE OF FLOOD EVENTS
Zubair woke up at dawn exhausted on a tract of land after clinging to a floating tree log all night.
He wept bitterly as he remembered his mother's hand slipping away in the dark, raging floodwaters.
Soldiers sailing in an emergency rescue boat spotted Zubair at sunset and transported him to safety.
At the relief camp, Zubair wondered why preventive plans were not taught to villagers every year.
A sympathetic relief worker joined hands with Zubair to draft clear flood safety guidelines on bedsheets.
They gathered camp residents and conducted awareness sessions to train people for future emergencies.
Q: How did Zubair reach the tract of land, and why was he weeping so sorrowfully?

Ans: Zubair reached the tract of land because the tree log he had held onto all night drifted toward the bank. He was crying bitterly because his beloved mother, the sole family member he had in the world, had slipped from his grip into the roaring dark waters and drowned.
Q: Who arrived to rescue Zubair, and where did they take him?

Ans: A team of vigilant army soldiers patrolling the floodwaters in an engine boat spotted Zubair in the dim light of dusk. They gently brought him aboard and transported him to a nearby emergency relief camp.
Q: What deep questions troubled Zubair's mind while walking around the relief camp?

Ans: Zubair was deeply troubled by thoughts such as: 'Why do we let this tragedy happen every monsoon season?', 'Why is there no early warning and disaster plan?', and 'What can we do ourselves so other innocent children do not become orphans?'
Q: How did Zubair and the young relief worker transform their thoughts into practical community action?

Ans: They refused to remain passive victims. Together, they compiled vital safety rules categorized into 'Before', 'During', and 'After' a flood. They wrote these rules in bold letters on large white bedsheets and held interactive training sessions to educate camp families.
Q: What lesson does this story teach about overcoming personal grief during national crises?

Ans: The story teaches that immense personal sorrow can be transformed into heroic social service. Instead of despairing, courageous individuals take initiative, educate their community, and build collective resilience to protect human lives from future natural disasters.
► 3.2 Speaking: Expressing Ability and Inability with Logical Reasons
• Speaking Focus: Modal Expressions of Ability and Inability
Use modal expressions of ability (can, could, able to) and inability (cannot, could not, unable to) supported by clear reasons:

• Dialogue 1: Evacuating safely during flash floodsRelief Worker: 'Could you walk through the flowing street water to reach the main road?'Villager: 'No, I could not walk through it because the water was flowing at high speed, and even six inches of rushing current can knock a grown person down.'

• Dialogue 2: Purifying drinking water in relief sheltersStudent A: 'Can we drink this tap water directly without boiling it?'Student B: 'No, we cannot drink it safely because floodwaters contaminate underground water pipes with sewage bacteria. We must boil it for at least ten minutes.'

• Dialogue 3: Swimming against heavy river currentsBoy: 'Were you able to swim across the swollen canal to save your goats?'Farmer: 'I was unable to do so because the gushing torrents carried floating logs and sharp debris, making swimming fatally hazardous.'
► 3.3 Language Practice: Zero and First Conditional Sentences
• Grammar Guide: Zero & First Conditional Sentences
1. Zero Conditional (Scientific truths, universal facts, rules):
• Structure: If / When + Present Simple, ... Present Simple.
• Example: If you heat water to 100 degrees Celsius, it boils.
• Example: If people drink contaminated floodwater, they fall ill.
2. First Conditional (Real or probable future situations and results):
• Structure: If + Present Simple, ... will / can / must + Base Verb.
• Example: If the river rises above the danger mark, authorities will order evacuation.
• Example: If you pack an emergency kit now, you will stay safe during disasters.
■ EXERCISE 1: ZERO CONDITIONAL SENTENCES (SCIENTIFIC & GENERAL TRUTHS)
Zero Conditional: (1) If heavy monsoon rains fall continuously, the mountain streams flood the valleys.
Zero Conditional: (2) When electrical appliances get wet, they cause dangerous short-circuits.
Zero Conditional: (3) If you boil water before drinking, harmful bacteria and germs die immediately.
Zero Conditional: (4) When soil loses its tree cover, severe land erosion takes place.
First Conditional: (1) If the meteorological department issues a flood warning, we will pack our emergency bags immediately.
First Conditional: (2) If we plant thousands of mangrove trees along the coast, they will protect our shoreline from tidal waves.
First Conditional: (3) If you touch a sagging electrical wire with a wet stick, you will receive a fatal electric shock.
First Conditional: (4) If community youth form rescue volunteer squads, they will save countless lives during emergencies.
First Conditional: (5) If people do not dump plastic bags in drains, city rainwater will drain away smoothly.
■ EXERCISE 3: CLAUSE ORDER INVERSION (NO COMMA NEEDED)
Transformation: Original (If-clause first)Inverted: If you listen to the radio alert, you will receive timely safety information.
Transformation: Inverted (Main clause first)Inverted: You will receive timely safety information if you listen to the radio alert. (Note: No comma needed)
► 3.4 Writing: Four-Paragraph Cause-and-Effect Essay on Natural Disasters
• Paragraph 1 (Introduction): Hook, general overview of natural calamities, and thesis statement.
• Paragraph 2 (Causes of Floods): Heavy monsoon rains, glacier melting, and lack of water storage dams.
• Paragraph 3 (Devastating Effects): Loss of human life, displacement, agricultural ruin, and epidemics.
• Paragraph 4 (Conclusion): Summary of key ideas, government preparedness, and civic responsibility.
■ MODEL EXPOSITORY ESSAY ON MONSOON FLOODS
• Model Essay: Monsoon Floods in Pakistan
Model Essay: Monsoon Floods in Pakistan — Causes, Effects, and Prevention

Natural calamities are unpredictable events of immense power that test human courage and societal resilience. Among all natural disasters, monsoon floods are the most recurrent and catastrophic crisis confronting Pakistan. Every few years, swelling rivers submerge vast plains, displacing millions of families and destroying infrastructure. Understanding the fundamental causes and disastrous consequences of floods is essential if our nation is to build effective protective strategies for the future.

The primary causes of recurrent flooding in Pakistan are both climatic and human-made. During the summer monsoon season, intense atmospheric depressions unleash torrential rains across northern mountain catchments. Simultaneously, rising global temperatures trigger rapid melting of northern glaciers, feeding enormous volumes of water into the Indus river system. This natural overflow is gravely aggravated by extensive deforestation along riverbanks, widespread siltation of riverbeds, and an acute shortage of modern storage reservoirs and dams to regulate excess water.

The consequences of these deluge torrents are catastrophic for both the national economy and human life. Entire villages are washed away within hours, drowning livestock and leaving hundreds of thousands of citizens homeless. Standing agricultural crops of cotton, rice, and sugarcane are wiped out, leading to food scarcity and economic inflation. Furthermore, stagnant floodwaters breed millions of mosquitoes and contaminate drinking wells, causing deadly outbreaks of malaria, dengue, typhoid, and cholera in crowded relief shelters.

In conclusion, while we cannot stop natural rain cycles, we can certainly prevent them from becoming deadly national catastrophes. The government must construct climate-resilient water reservoirs, strengthen river embankments, and enforce strict bans on illegal construction in natural waterways. Equally important is educating citizens on emergency preparedness, early evacuation, and basic first aid. By combining wise engineering with proactive community awareness, Pakistan can protect its people and land from the wrath of future floods.
► 3.5 Study Skills: Mastering Dictionary Skills for Language Growth
1. Guide Words: Look at the top of the dictionary page to know the first and last word on that page.
2. Alphabetical Order: Words are arranged from A to Z; look at the second, third, and fourth letters to find words quickly.
3. Part of Speech: Abbreviations like (n.) noun, (v.) verb, (adj.) adjective show how the word behaves in grammar.
4. Pronunciation & Syllable Division: Dots or slashes show how words break into spoken beats (e.g., ca-lam-i-ty).
An event that brings great loss, grief, or disaster.
To withdraw or remove people from a dangerous zone.
To cover completely with water or another liquid.
A fast-moving and violently rushing stream of water.
► 3.6 Fun Time: Emergency Grab-Bag Survival Checklist
Draw an 'Emergency Disaster Go-Bag' in your notebook and pack these essential items:
☑ 1. Waterproof Torch / Flashlight with extra alkaline batteries.
☑ 2. Small Battery-Powered Portable AM/FM Radio for emergency news broadcasts.
☑ 3. First Aid Kit (bandages, antiseptic lotion, burn cream, pain relievers).
☑ 4. Three-day supply of Water Purification Halazone Tablets.
☑ 5. Ready-to-eat dry rations (roasted grams, biscuits, dried dates).
☑ 6. Waterproof pouch containing original CNIC, B-forms, and school certificates.
☑ 7. High-frequency Emergency Safety Whistle to attract rescue boats in the dark.

content.text: THE MASTER SAHIB EDUCATIONAL SERIESCLASS VII ENGLISH — UNIT 4AWARENESS OF AND EMPATHY WITH SPECIAL PEOPLE(Complete Solved Textbook Exercises)
■  UNIT 4: AWARENESS OF AND EMPATHY WITH SPECIAL PEOPLE (SOLVED TEXTBOOK EXERCISES)
► 4.1 Reading Comprehension: The Blind Boy (Poem by Colley Cibber)
Exploring empathy, sensory perception, and understanding special abilities:
Pre-Reading Q1. Did you know that you have not tasted the king of fruits (the durian)? Does it make any difference to your happiness?
Ans: No, it makes no difference whatsoever to my daily happiness. Since I have never tasted or seen it, I do not feel any sense of deprivation or sorrow over its absence.
Pre-Reading Q2. When babies are born without sight or hearing, do they know what they are missing?
Ans: No, infants born without sight or hearing do not know what visual or auditory sensations feel like. Their inner world is formed through touch, smell, warmth, and sound vibrations.
Pre-Reading Q3. By what age do you think they begin to know that they are different from others?

Ans: Around the age of four to six, when they begin socializing with other children, going to kindergarten, or hearing people describe visual colours and sights, they gradually realize their unique condition.
Pre-Reading Q4. Is it easy for them to understand what they are missing? Why / Why not?

Ans: It is conceptually very difficult for them to picture sight because vision has no equivalent in darkness. Just as we cannot comprehend a sixth sense we do not possess, a person blind from birth perceives light merely as radiant warmth, not as a visual image.
■ WHILE-READING EXERCISE 1: YES / NO FACTUAL QUESTIONS
Item: 1. Was the boy blind from birth? → Yes — The poem indicates he never enjoyed the blessings of sight.
Item: 2. Was he happy and content? → Yes — He maintains a joyful and cheerful mind despite his blindness.
Item: 3. Did he know the true visual difference between light and darkness? → No — He can only feel the warmth of the sun, not see its illumination.
Item: 4. Is the blind boy's father telling us the story? → No — The blind boy himself is speaking directly to the reader in the first person ('I').
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 2: POETIC VOCABULARY IN CONTEXT
a favour, gift, or divine mercy from God
inspiring awe, marvel, or great wonder
feel or express deep sorrow and grief over a loss
great sorrow, grief, or deep distress
ability to endure hardship calmly without complaint
joyful, cheerful, and peaceful state of mind
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 3: VOCABULARY FILL IN THE BLANKS
Solved Blank: (1) In the final football matches, he always loses in a hapless manner.
Solved Blank: (2) He misses his father so let's do something to cheer his heavy heart.
Solved Blank: (3) There are many wondrous and majestic creations to observe in nature.
Solved Blank: (4) We should show immense patience when frail elderly people do not understand us.
Solved Blank: (5) When we pray sincerely, we receive Allah's boundless blessings.
Solved Blank: (6) We should not always mourn bitterly whenever we suffer a temporary worldly loss.
Solved Blank: (7) Sadia was weeping softly and narrating her painful story of woe to her teachers.
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 4: RHYMING PAIRS & SOUND PATTERNS
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 5: POETIC CONTRACTED SHORT FORMS
Contraction: 'whilst' = while / at the same time
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 6 & 7: TRUE OR FALSE STATEMENTS
The blind boy feels miserable and spends all his time weeping in a corner.
False — He is remarkably cheerful and sings happily like a king.
He creates his own day and night according to when he plays or sleeps.
True — Since he cannot see sunlight, he defines day as his playtime and night as his sleep time.
People around the blind boy often sigh and express pity over his blindness.
True — Hearing heavy sighs from well-wishers is how he learns about his supposed misfortune.
The blind boy wants to destroy his peace of mind by longing for things he can never have.
False — He deliberately resolves never to let unattainable sights destroy his cheerful mind.
The poem was written by the famous English poet and dramatist Colley Cibber.
True — C. Cibber composed this moving and inspiring lyrical poem.
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 8 & 9: GAPPED SUMMARY OF THE POEM
• Gapped Summary of the Poem: The Blind Boy

In this touching poem, a blind boy expresses his feelings about his condition. He has never experienced the gift of (1) [sight] and cannot understand the mysterious thing called (2) [light]. Sighted people tell him that the sun shines (3) [bright], but the boy can only feel its (4) [warmth]. Therefore, he makes his own day and night: whenever he plays, it is (5) [day], and whenever he sleeps, it is (6) [night]. Although he hears others heavily (7) [sigh] and mourn his unlucky loss, he bears his condition with noble (8) [patience]. He refuses to let what he cannot have destroy his inner (9) [cheer] of mind. While he sings with a contented spirit, he feels as proud and happy as a (10) [king].
sight, light, bright, warmth, day, night, sigh, patience, cheer, king
Q: How does the blind boy understand and distinguish between day and night?

Ans: Since the blind boy has never seen the sun's illumination, he cannot distinguish day and night through visual light. Instead, he defines day and night by his personal activities: whenever he is awake and playing, he considers it day; whenever he sleeps, it is night for him.
Q: Why does the blind boy bear his blindness with patience and without complaint?

Ans: He bears his blindness calmly because he has never experienced visual sight, and therefore cannot mourn what he never knew. He reasons that it is foolish to grieve over an unattainable blessing when one can enjoy life through touch, sound, and a cheerful imagination.
Q: Why does the boy say 'Whilst thus I sing, I am a king, although a poor blind boy'?

Ans: A king possesses inner contentment, pride, and total mastery over his realm. The blind boy, by ruling over his own mind and refusing to allow grief or self-pity to defeat him, feels richer and happier than an earthly monarch, proving that true happiness lies in mental attitude.
Q: What lesson does the poem teach about treating differently-abled people?

Ans: The poem teaches that differently-abled persons do not need pity, sorrowful sighs, or patronizing tears. They deserve respect, encouragement, equal educational opportunities, and an environment that celebrates their unique abilities, dignity, and high spirits.
• Speaking Focus: Expressing Surprise and Admiration
Everyday conversational expressions used to express surprise, awe, and admiration:
• 'Really?!', • 'Good heavens!', • 'What a pleasant surprise!', • 'Are you serious?', • 'How wonderful!'

• Dialogue 1: Learning about a blind boy's academic triumphFarhan: 'Did you know that Asad, who is completely blind, secured first position in the English speech contest?'Bilal: 'Good heavens! What an extraordinary achievement! He memorized the entire five-page speech by listening to audio recordings.'

• Dialogue 2: Discovering braille reading capabilityZainab: 'Look at how fast Maryam is reading that thick book with the tips of her fingers!'Ayesha: 'Really?! That is truly amazing! That raised dot system is called Braille, and she reads it faster than sighted people read print.'

• Dialogue 3: Differently-abled athlete winning a gold medalHamza: 'Our school wheelchair cricket team defeated the district champions today!'Kamal: 'Wow, what fantastic news! Their courage and determination are truly inspiring for all of us.'
► 4.3 Language Practice: Forming Adjectives & Question Words
■ EXERCISE 1: FORMING ADJECTIVES FROM NOUNS USING SUFFIXES (-FUL, -LESS, -ABLE, -OUS)
The blind boy marvels at the wondrous warmth of the sun.
He maintains a cheerful disposition in every trial.
Sighted people mistakenly think the blind boy is helpless.
A patient heart overcomes every physical disability.
Walking alone near open construction trenches is dangerous.
The students achieved a glorious victory in the debate.
We must make school classrooms comfortable for wheelchair users.
A clean mind leads to a peaceful and contented life.
Careless disposal of sharp glass injures pedestrians.
Big Brother provided valuable tips on social manners.
■ EXERCISE 2: EXTENDED USE OF QUESTION WORDS (WH- QUESTIONS)
Question: (1) What does the blind boy wonder about the mysterious thing called light?
Question: (2) Who composed the inspirational poem 'The Blind Boy'? (Colley Cibber)
Question: (3) When does the blind boy decide that it is daytime? (When he plays)
Question: (4) Where do special students learn reading through the raised dot alphabet? (In specialized schools)
Question: (5) Why does the boy refuse to let pity destroy his peace of mind? (Because he values contentment)
Question: (6) How can sighted citizens make public transport accessible for the visually impaired? (By offering guided assistance)
Question: (7) Whose heavy sighs does the boy often hear? (The sighs of sympathetic onlookers)
► 4.4 Writing: Cause-and-Effect Essay on Empathy with Special People
• Essay Writing Guidelines on Social Inclusion
• Introductory Paragraph: Define special abilities; contrast destructive pity with empowering empathy.
• Body Paragraph 1 (Causes of Difficulties): Inaccessible buildings, social neglect, and lack of ramps.
• Body Paragraph 2 (Effects of Empathy & Inclusion): Self-reliance, psychological confidence, and national contribution.
• Concluding Paragraph: Call to action for inclusive educational facilities, braille signage, and equal rights.
■ MODEL CAUSE-AND-EFFECT ESSAY ON EMPATHY WITH SPECIAL PEOPLE
• Model Essay: Fostering Empathy for Special People
Model Essay: Fostering Empathy and Inclusivity for Special People in Society

Every society is judged by how compassionately and justly it treats its most vulnerable members. Differently-abled individuals, including those who cannot see, hear, or walk without assistance, possess the exact same intellectual brilliance, emotional depth, and human potential as any other citizen. However, they frequently encounter social exclusion not because of their personal physical limitations, but because society fails to build an empathetic and supportive environment. Developing true empathy, rather than hollow pity, is a moral imperative for building an enlightened nation.

The primary obstacles confronting special people stem directly from physical and institutional barriers. Public schools, transport terminals, pedestrian bridges, and government offices in Pakistan are rarely designed with wheelchair ramps, tactile braille paving, or acoustic pedestrian signals. Consequently, visually impaired and mobility-challenged individuals struggle constantly with basic navigation. Furthermore, societal ignorance often stereotypes differently-abled citizens as helpless objects of charity, denying them standard classroom education and respectable white-collar employment.

The positive effects of removing these barriers and extending sincere empathy are transformative. When schools introduce braille textbooks, sign language interpreters, and ramped entrances, special students excel in science, arts, and technology, frequently outperforming their peers. Gaining education fosters financial self-reliance and profound self-dignity, liberating individuals from the burden of dependence. History abounds with luminous examples, such as Helen Keller and Stephen Hawking, demonstrating that physical hurdles cannot shackle the soaring human intellect when opportunities are provided.

In conclusion, differently-abled people do not crave sorrowful tears or charity; they demand accessibility, equality, and unshakeable respect. Our government must strictly mandate universal accessibility designs in all public architecture and commercial transport. Simultaneously, families and educational institutions must educate young minds to welcome, assist, and celebrate friends with special needs. By embracing every citizen with dignity and love, Pakistan will become an inclusive haven where all individuals can rise to their fullest potential.
► 4.5 Study Skills: Reading and Analysing Book Blurbs
A 'blurb' is a short, captivating summary written on the back cover of a book to give readers a preview of the plot and themes without giving away the ending:
Sample Book Blurb: 'Beyond the Shadows' by Dr. Tariq Mansoor

Twelve-year-old Daniyal has never seen the green colour of grass or the blue expanse of the ocean. Blind since birth, he navigates his mountain village using sound echoes and his loyal German Shepherd, Sheru. But when an unexpected flash flood threatens to wash away the wooden suspension bridge connecting his village to the district hospital, Daniyal is the only one who can navigate the dark, stormy cliffs by touch to deliver the emergency distress beacon.
A breathtaking tale of grit, unwavering courage, and the triumph of the human spirit over physical darkness. 'A masterpiece of hope that will inspire every young reader!' — The Daily Dawn.
Analysis: Q: 1. What is the title and author of the book?A: 'Beyond the Shadows' by Dr. Tariq Mansoor.
Analysis: Q: 2. Who is the central character and what is his special condition?A: Daniyal, a brave twelve-year-old boy who is visually impaired from birth.
Analysis: Q: 3. What is the central dramatic crisis described in the blurb?A: A flash flood threatens the village suspension bridge, and Daniyal must navigate stormy cliffs in the dark.

Analysis: Q: 4. Why does this blurb make readers want to buy the book?A: It creates intense suspense and portrays a differently-abled protagonist performing heroic feats, inspiring deep curiosity about the ending.
E — Everyone deserves respect and understanding.
M — Making classrooms accessible for all friends.
P — Patience and kindness in every conversation.
A — Always lending a warm, helping hand.
T — Treating every human being with dignity.
H — Hearing the unspoken emotions of others.
Y — You and I can build an inclusive world!

content.text: THE MASTER SAHIB EDUCATIONAL SERIESCLASS VII ENGLISH — UNIT 5HISTORICAL AND CULTURAL PLACES OF PAKISTAN(Complete Solved Textbook Exercises)
■  UNIT 5: HISTORICAL AND CULTURAL PLACES OF PAKISTAN (SOLVED TEXTBOOK EXERCISES)
► 5.1 Reading Comprehension: Pakistan: Home to Ancient Civilizations (Helicopter Aerial Tour)
Exploring archaeological heritage, ancient cultures, and national history:
Pre-Reading Q1. What is history, and why do we study it?

Ans: History is the chronological record of past human events, cultures, inventions, and civilizations. We study history to understand our cultural roots, learn from previous societies' achievements and failures, and preserve national identity for future generations.
Pre-Reading Q2. Can you name some prominent historical and heritage places across the provinces of Pakistan?

Ans: Famous heritage sites in Pakistan include Mohenjo-Daro and Bhambore in Sindh, Harappa and Taxila in Punjab, Takht-i-Bahi in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Nindowari and Mehrgarh in Balochistan, alongside iconic monuments like Lahore Fort and the Badshahi Mosque.
Pre-Reading Q3. Why is Pakistan considered one of the most culturally ancient lands in the world?

Ans: Pakistan is home to the Indus Valley Civilization—one of the earliest major urban settlements in human history—dating back more than five thousand years, alongside prehistoric Neolithic settlements and Buddhist, Hindu, and early Islamic heritage.
■ WHILE-READING EXERCISE 1: AERIAL HELICOPTER TOUR OVERVIEW
Q: How many ancient historical sites did the helicopter aerial tour visit across Pakistan, and in which provinces are they located?

Ans: The two-day helicopter tour visited six major archaeological sites across all four provinces:1. Bhambore (Thatta, Sindh)2. Mohenjo-Daro (Larkana, Sindh)3. Nindowari (Kalat, Balochistan)4. Harappa (Sahiwal, Punjab)5. Taxila (Rawalpindi, Punjab)6. Takht-i-Bahi (Mardan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa).
an advanced stage of human social and cultural development
left completely empty, deserted, and uninhabited
having the shape of half a circle
the period of human history before written records existed
a large raised pile or hill of earth or stones covering ruins
protected with strong defensive walls and gates against attack
a period of one thousand years (plural: millennia)
dug out carefully from the ground to reveal ancient ruins
relating to monks, religious meditation, and monasteries
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 3 & 4: ANCIENT HISTORICAL SITES COMPARISON TABLE
Ancient coastal port on Gharo creek; features three periods: a semi-circular stone palace, a Hindu Shiva temple, and one of the region's earliest mosques (dated 727 AD).
Major metropolis of Indus Valley Civilization; famous for grid-plan streets, public wells, Great Bath, and sophisticated underground covered drainage system.
Prehistoric Kulli culture settlement built on a flat rock; features a large central square platform and an 82-foot high stone mound.
Bronze Age fortified urban city; famous for massive granaries, clay seals, and evidence of international trade along the Ravi river.
Meaning 'City of Cut Stone'; ancient seat of Gandhara art and Buddhist learning; features three sequential cities (Bhir Mound, Sirkap, Sirsukh) destroyed by Huns.
Magnificent Buddhist monastic complex perched 500 feet atop a hill; exceptionally well-preserved stupas, monk cells, and meditation halls.
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 5: TRUE OR FALSE STATEMENTS
Bhambore was abandoned in the 13th century because the course of the River Indus shifted.
True — The shift in river direction cut off its freshwater and harbour connection.
Mohenjo-Daro lacked any planning and had dirty, open wastewater flowing in streets.
False — It was an extraordinarily well-planned city with covered drains lining every major street.
Nindowari is an ancient Greek settlement located near the Arabian Sea.
False — It belongs to the prehistoric Kulli culture of Balochistan in the Ornach Valley.
Taxila was destroyed in the fifth century AD by invading White Huns.
True — The fierce invasion of the Huns brought an end to Taxila's intellectual glory.
Takht-i-Bahi is located on the seashore near Gwadar port.
False — It is a hilltop Buddhist monastery located near Mardan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Q: Why was the ancient coastal city of Bhambore abandoned after the 13th Century?

Ans: Bhambore was gradually abandoned after the 13th Century AD primarily because the River Indus changed its course and delta channels, cutting off the city from essential freshwater supplies and silting up its busy seaport harbour.
Q: What architectural evidence proves that Mohenjo-Daro was a highly organized modern city?

Ans: Archaeological evidence includes wide straight streets laid out in a precise grid pattern, standardized baked bricks, a central public marketplace, numerous freshwater wells, private bathrooms in multi-storey houses, and an advanced network of covered brick drains running beneath street pavements.
Q: Why did the ancient settlement of Nindowari decline around 2500 BC?

Ans: Geological movements caused the surrounding land to rise, which permanently cut off the settlement from its primary water lifeline, the Kud River, making agriculture and daily survival impossible.
Q: Explain the historical significance of Taxila as a centre of learning and commerce.

Ans: Taxila, situated at the crossroads of ancient Silk Route trade corridors between the Indian subcontinent, Central Asia, and Persia, was a world-renowned centre of Gandhara sculpture, philosophy, medicine, and university learning that attracted scholars across Asia.
Q: Why has the monastic complex of Takht-i-Bahi survived in such remarkably good condition?

Ans: Because it was constructed atop a secluded, breezy hill roughly 500 feet high, away from seasonal river floods and warfare ravages. Its thick stone masonry and protected location allowed its stupas and monk cells to survive intact for centuries.
► 5.2 Speaking: Expressing Pleasure and Displeasure Politely
• Speaking Focus: Expressing Pleasure and Displeasure Politely
Useful phrases for expressing delight/pleasure vs polite displeasure:
• Pleasure: 'I am absolutely delighted!', 'What a marvelous sight!', 'It gives me immense pleasure.'
• Displeasure: 'I am deeply saddened to see this.', 'It is truly disappointing.', 'I must express my displeasure about...'

• Dialogue 1: Visiting Mohenjo-daro MuseumTourist: 'I am absolutely thrilled by the sophisticated brick architecture of Mohenjo-daro! It gives me immense pleasure to see our ancestors were so advanced.'Guide: 'Indeed, sir! But I feel deep displeasure when careless tourists carve graffiti on these ancient walls and discard plastic bottles around the Great Bath.'

• Dialogue 2: School excursion to Taxila MuseumTeacher: 'Look at the exquisite details on this carved stone Buddha statue from Gandhara.'Student: 'What a marvelous sight! It is such a joy to study our history in person rather than just reading dry textbook chapters.'
► 5.3 Language Practice: Present Perfect Tense & Rules of Article 'The'
Grammar Guide for Present Perfect Tense:
• Structure: Subject + has / have + Past Participle (V3).
- Singular subjects (He, She, It, singular noun) take 'has' (e.g., He has visited Taxila).
- Plural subjects (I, We, You, They, plural nouns) take 'have' (e.g., Archaeologists have excavated Harappa).
• Function: Describes actions completed recently, past actions with present consequences, or life experiences.
■ EXERCISE 1: PRESENT PERFECT TENSE SENTENCE COMPLETION
Present Perfect: (1) Archaeologists (excavate) have excavated magnificent stone stupas at Takht-i-Bahi.
Present Perfect: (2) The federal government (declare) has declared Mohenjo-Daro a protected national heritage site.
Present Perfect: (3) Our school history class (visit) has visited the Thatta museum twice this year.
Present Perfect: (4) UNESCO (recognize) has recognized six cultural sites in Pakistan on its World Heritage List.
Present Perfect: (5) I (read, not) have not read the full excavation report on Bhambore yet.
Present Perfect: (6) The museum curator (restore) has restored the antique pottery jars found in Harappa.
■ EXERCISE 2: RULES AND APPLICATION OF THE DEFINITE ARTICLE 'THE'
• Rules for Article 'The' with Geographical Features
• Use 'The' with: Rivers (the Indus, the Ravi), Seas/Oceans (the Arabian Sea), Mountain ranges (the Himalayas), Desert names (the Thar), and Specific monuments (the Badshahi Mosque).

• Do NOT use 'The' with: Individual lakes (Lake Saiful Muluk), Single mountain peaks (K2, Mount Everest), Continents (Asia), or Single countries (Pakistan, China) unless the name includes words like Republic, Kingdom, or States (e.g., the United States).
Article Usage: (1) Bhambore is situated on the northern bank of the Gharo creek.
Article Usage: (2) Mohenjo-Daro was built beside the Indus River.
Article Usage: (3) Harappa flourished in the fertile valley of the Ravi.
Article Usage: (4) We visited Taxila (No article) in Punjab last winter.
Article Usage: (5) Ancient trade moved across the Arabian Sea to Middle Eastern ports.
► 5.4 Writing: Formal and Informal E-mails on Cultural Heritage
• Standard Format and Guidelines for E-mail Writing
• Subject: Concise, clear, and informative line summarizing the email purpose.
• Salutation: Respectful greeting ('Dear Sir/Madam,' for formal; 'Dear Liam,' for informal).
• Body: Divided into introductory purpose, detailed facts/request, and courteous closing.
• Sign-off: 'Sincerely, / Best regards,' followed by sender's name and designation.
■ MODEL INFORMAL E-MAIL: INVITING AN INTERNATIONAL FRIEND TO VISIT ANCIENT SITES
Model Informal E-mail: Inviting an International Pen-Pal to Visit Ancient Sites of Pakistan
Subject: Invitation to Explore Ancient Civilizations in Pakistan!

I hope this email finds you in high spirits and good health! I am writing to invite you to visit Pakistan during your upcoming winter break. Knowing how passionate you are about archaeology and ancient history, I promise you will have the journey of a lifetime.

Did you know that Pakistan is home to the ancient Indus Valley Civilization? My family is planning a road trip to Mohenjo-Daro in Sindh and the Gandhara ruins of Taxila near Islamabad. You will see 5,000-year-old cities with covered underground drainage, public baths, and beautiful terracotta pottery. You can stay with us in Karachi, and my parents will ensure you enjoy authentic Sindhi hospitality and delicious traditional cuisine.
Please check with your parents and confirm your flight schedule so I can finalize our tour bookings. Looking forward to welcoming you soon!
■ MODEL FORMAL E-MAIL: REQUESTING GUIDED MUSEUM TOUR FOR STUDENTS
Model Formal E-mail: Requesting Guided Student Tour of the Taxila Museum
Subject: Request for Guided Educational Tour for Class VII Students

I am writing on behalf of the Social Studies Society of Government Boys Secondary School, Rawalpindi. As part of our annual cultural curriculum, we have scheduled an educational excursion to Taxila Museum and the Sirkap archaeological site on Friday, 15th October 2026.

A group of forty students from Class VII, accompanied by three senior history teachers, will be visiting between 10:00 am and 1:30 pm. We kindly request the museum administration to provide a designated historical guide who can explain the significance of the Gandhara Buddhist sculptures and the three ancient city ruins to our young students.
Kindly confirm if student concession tickets are available and inform us of any specific photography or museum rules we should observe during our visit. Thank you for your time and cooperation.
► 5.5 Study Skills: Reading and Navigating a Book Content Page
• Study Skills: Navigating a Book Content Page

The Table of Contents gives a structured roadmap of a book. It helps readers quickly locate units, themes, sub-topics, and corresponding page numbers without flipping aimlessly through hundreds of pages:

content.text: THE MASTER SAHIB EDUCATIONAL SERIESCLASS VII ENGLISH — UNIT 6MEDIA AS A SOURCE OF KNOWLEDGE(Complete Solved Textbook Exercises)
■  UNIT 6: MEDIA AS A SOURCE OF KNOWLEDGE (SOLVED TEXTBOOK EXERCISES)
► 6.1 Reading Comprehension: Different Newspaper News (Authentic Press Reports)
Understanding modern news media, credibility, and journalistic components:
Pre-Reading Q1. Do you read newspapers? Why? Why not?
Ans: Yes, I read the daily newspaper regularly because it keeps me informed about national events, scientific breakthroughs, weather forecasts, educational competitions, and global current affairs.
Pre-Reading Q2. Do you think people should read newspapers in this digital age? Why?

Ans: Yes, absolutely. While social media is full of unverified rumours and clickbait, credible printed and online newspapers provide professionally researched, fact-checked reporting and balanced editorial opinions.
Pre-Reading Q3. What key components make up a typical newspaper news item?

Ans: A standard news report includes an attention-grabbing Headline, a Dateline (city name and date), a Lead paragraph answering the 5 Ws and 1 H, supporting body details, official quotes, and background context.
■ WHILE-READING EXERCISE 1: MATCHING HEADLINES TO EVENTS
Headline Match: News Item 1: Youth, nephew drown in rainwater pond (Mirpurkhas village tragedy)
Headline Match: News Item 2: Names that reflect our heritage (Children's Literature Festival in Islamabad)
Headline Match: News Item 3: Zookeeper injured by big cat (Safety breach at zoo enclosure)
Headline Match: News Item 4: Dengue awareness walk held in Talash (Community health mobilization in Dir)
Headline Match: News Item 5: Woman, 3 children burnt in fire (Domestic gas cylinder leakage incident)
■ POST-READING EXERCISE 2: NEWS ANALYSIS TABLE (THE 5 WS AND 1 H)
15-year-old Bhutta Khan and 5-year-old nephew Mohsin Khan.
Drowned tragically in an open rainwater pond; three other children rescued.
Noor Mohammed Moosapota village, near Digri town, Mirpurkhas.

Zoo attendant and an adult male Bengal tiger.
Attendant suffered severe arm injuries while pushing meat into the cage.

Early morning; gas accumulated overnight from a faulty stove valve.
died through being submerged in water and unable to breathe
sufficiently great or important to be worthy of attention

treasured historical tradition of writing, poetry, and books
not giving sufficient attention or thought to safety

■ POST-READING EXERCISE 4: FACT VS OPINION IDENTIFICATION IN MEDIA
Media Literacy: (1) "Two children died after falling into an open rainwater pond."Analysis: Fact — A verified, documented tragedy confirmed by hospital authorities.
Media Literacy: (2) "Naming conference rooms after national heroes is the best idea in festival history."Analysis: Opinion — A subjective value judgment expressing an organizer's personal admiration.
Media Literacy: (3) "The tiger attacked the attendant during morning feeding hours."Analysis: Fact — An objective, observable event that took place at the zoo enclosure.
Media Literacy: (4) "The zookeeper was careless and deserved the injury."Analysis: Opinion — A biased personal judgment rather than an official investigative report.
Media Literacy: (5) "Dengue mosquitoes breed in clean, stagnant pools of rainwater."Analysis: Fact — A proven scientific biological reality verified by medical research.
Q: Why should open rainwater ponds and construction pits in villages be fenced securely?

Ans: Open rainwater ponds in rural villages pose lethal hazards for playing children who cannot gauge water depth or mud suction. Installing sturdy wire fences and warning signs prevents tragic drowning deaths like the Mirpurkhas incident.
Q: What positive educational purpose was served by naming festival halls after literary icons?

Ans: Naming rooms after Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, Allama Iqbal, Saadat Hasan Manto, and Arfa Karim actively introduces young generations to Pakistan's rich philosophical, poetic, and technological heritage, inspiring pride and cultural literacy.
Q: What safety failure led to the zookeeper being mauled at the zoo, and how can it be avoided?

Ans: The zookeeper violated mandatory safety protocols by failing to slide and lock the secondary iron partition before entering the feeding grill. Such accidents can be prevented through double-door interlocking mechanisms, mandatory partner supervision, and rigorous safety audits.
Q: What practical advice did participants in the Talash walk share to eliminate dengue?

Ans: Participants urged citizens to empty and scrub water containers weekly, replace cooler water, remove discarded tires and plastic cups where water stagnates, and report uncollected garbage heaps to local health authorities.
Q: What vital precautions should every household observe regarding domestic gas appliances?

Ans: Families must ensure rooms are well-ventilated, inspect rubber gas pipes and regulator valves regularly for leaks using soapy water (never a naked flame), and always turn off the cylinder knob completely before going to bed.
► 6.2 Speaking: Expressing Disappointment and Sympathy Courteously
• Speaking Focus: Expressing Disappointment and Sympathy
Phrases for expressing regret, disappointment, and sympathy:
• 'What a terrible tragedy!', • 'I am deeply saddened to hear this.', • 'How disappointing that safety rules were ignored.', • 'What a pity!'

• Dialogue 1: Discussing the village pond accidentStudent A: 'Did you read about the two young boys who drowned in an unfenced pond in Digri?'Student B: 'What a heartbreaking tragedy! It is truly disappointing that local authorities did not erect safety fences around such deep rainwater pits.'

• Dialogue 2: Expressing dismay over the zoo accidentStudent A: 'The zoo attendant was severely mauled by a tiger because he forgot to lock the safety gate.'Student B: 'What a pity! How disappointing that trained staff still neglect basic life-saving protocols in wild animal enclosures.'
► 6.3 Language Practice: Use of 'Since' vs 'For' & Indirect Speech for Orders
Grammar Guide for Since and For:
• 'Since': Used to specify a starting point in time (e.g., since Monday, since 2018, since 8:00 am, since yesterday, since childhood).
• 'For': Used to specify a duration or period of time (e.g., for three hours, for five days, for ten months, for two years, for a long time).
Tense Exercise: (1) The village volunteers have been patrolling the pond since Friday morning.
Tense Exercise: (2) The injured children stayed in the emergency ward for three days.
Tense Exercise: (3) The Children's Literature Festival has been promoting books since 2011.
Tense Exercise: (4) Doctors have conducted anti-dengue walks in Lower Dir for two consecutive weeks.
Tense Exercise: (5) The family has lived in that residential apartment for ten years.
Tense Exercise: (6) Water has been leaking from the municipal pipeline since last night.
Tense Exercise: (7) The zookeeper has worked at the botanical garden since January.
■ EXERCISE 2: INDIRECT SPEECH FOR ORDERS AND REQUESTS
• Rules for Reporting Orders and Requests
Rules for Reporting Orders and Requests into Indirect Speech:
• Change reporting verb 'said to' into 'ordered', 'commanded', 'requested', or 'advised'.
• Remove quotation marks and insert 'to' before the main verb (or 'not to' for negative imperatives).
• Example: The officer said to the rescuer, 'Jump into the water immediately!'
→ The officer ordered the rescuer to jump into the water immediately.
Narration Transformation: Direct: The doctor said to the patient, 'Drink only boiled water during monsoon.'Indirect: The doctor advised the patient to drink only boiled water during monsoon.
Narration Transformation: Direct: The zookeeper said to visitors, 'Please do not tease the animals.'Indirect: The zookeeper requested the visitors not to tease the animals.

Narration Transformation: Direct: The teacher said to students, 'Form an orderly queue before boarding the bus.'Indirect: The teacher ordered the students to form an orderly queue before boarding the bus.
Narration Transformation: Direct: Mother said to Ali, 'Check the gas stove valve before sleeping.'Indirect: Mother instructed Ali to check the gas stove valve before sleeping.
► 6.4 Writing: Producing an Authentic Newspaper Report
1. Headline: Bold, short, active present tense to grab attention.
2. Byline & Dateline: Author's credit, city name, and date of report.
3. Lead Paragraph: Crucial summary answering Who, What, Where, When, and Why in 1–2 sentences.
4. Body Paragraphs: Background details, official statements, and eyewitness quotes.
5. Concluding Sentence: Current status or future preventive action.
• Model Report: Student Tree Plantation Drive
Model Newspaper Report: School Launches Green Campus Initiative
STUDENTS PLANT 1,000 SAPLINGS IN MASSIVE CIVIC DRIVE

In an inspiring community effort to combat urban heat waves and rising air pollution, over five hundred students of Government Boys Secondary School launched a massive 'Green Sindh' tree plantation drive across the city today.

The drive commenced early Friday morning under the supervision of the District Forest Officer and school faculty. Students planted one thousand indigenous shade-giving neem, gulmohar, and lignum saplings along school grounds, public park perimeters, and roadside dividers. Each classroom adopted twenty saplings and pledged to water and care for them daily.

'Our youth are not just reading about environmental science in textbooks; they are taking practical stewardship of their planet,' stated Headmaster Mr. Tariq Peerzada while addressing the closing assembly. Local municipal representatives commended the initiative and announced plans to install drip irrigation pipes along the planted avenues.
► 6.5 Study Skills: Critical Reading of Newspaper Headlines & Media Blurbs
• Study Skills: Critical Analysis of Headlines
• Headline Grammar: Headlines frequently omit articles (a, an, the) and auxiliary verbs ('is', 'are') to conserve space (e.g., 'Youth Drowns' instead of 'A Youth Has Drowned').
• Fact vs Sensationalism: Look for factual data, named witnesses, and verifiable sources rather than sensational adjectives.
• Reading for Gist: Skim the first two paragraphs of any news item to grasp eighty percent of the essential story.
A dengue awareness walk was held in Talash.
A woman and three children were burnt in a fire.
A zookeeper was injured by a tiger.
► 6.6 Fun Time: Media Crossword Clues & Riddles
Media Riddle: Riddle 1: I have sheets, but no bed; I have headlines, but no brain; I tell you yesterday's news today. What am I?Answer: A Newspaper.
Media Riddle: Riddle 2: I am printed on the front page in the largest, boldest letters to scream the biggest story. What am I?Answer: The Headline.
Media Riddle: Riddle 3: I travel everywhere with a camera and notebook, asking questions that make corrupt people tremble. What am I?Answer: An Investigative Journalist.
