content.text: THE MASTER SAHIB EDUCATIONAL SERIESCLASS IX ENGLISH — UNIT 5HEALTHY LIFE STYLE(Complete Solved Textbook Exercises)
■  UNIT 5: HEALTHY LIFE STYLE (SOLVED TEXTBOOK EXERCISES)
► 5.1 Reading Comprehension: Health Problems Caused by Mosquitoes (Malaria & Dengue Prevention)
Pre-Reading Q1. Why are mosquitoes considered among the deadliest creatures on Earth?

Ans: Despite their tiny size, mosquitoes act as biological vectors transmitting lethal pathogens and parasites that cause widespread infectious diseases such as Malaria, Dengue fever, Yellow fever, and Chikungunya.
Pre-Reading Q2. What environmental conditions facilitate the rapid breeding of mosquitoes in our towns?
Ans: Stagnant rainwater, uncovered water storage tanks, clogged drainage gutters, discarded plastic tires, and uncollected trash create ideal stagnant breeding grounds for mosquito larvae.
■ VOCABULARY EXERCISE 2: MEDICAL & BIOLOGICAL TERMINOLOGY TABLE
An organism (like a mosquito) that transmits pathogens from one host to another
Water that is standing still, not flowing, and often dirty or foul-smelling
A microscopic organism that lives inside a host and causes disease
The active immature worm-like stage of an insect before metamorphosis
The process of spraying chemical insecticide smoke to eradicate adult mosquitoes
A widespread occurrence of an infectious disease in a community at a particular time
The biological ability of the body to resist infection or disease toxins
The number of blood-clotting cells in the blood, which drops sharply during Dengue
Female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit the malaria parasite Plasmodium.
The Aedes mosquito breeds in clean, stagnant water and bites primarily during daylight hours.
Mosquitoes can breed in rapidly flowing river waters.
False (F) — Mosquitoes require calm, stagnant water to lay eggs and hatch larvae.
Dengue fever causes high fever, severe joint pain, rash, and a drastic drop in blood platelets.
Using insect repellents and sleeping under mosquito nets helps prevent mosquito bites.
MCQ 1. Which mosquito species is the primary carrier of the Dengue virus?  • a. Male Anopheles  • b. Aedes aegypti (Tiger mosquito)  • c. Culex mosquito  • d. Housefly

MCQ 2. What is the most effective community method to prevent mosquito proliferation?  • a. Leaving water tanks open  • b. Eliminating stagnant standing water and covering water containers  • c. Cutting green trees  • d. Storing water in discarded tires
Ans: b. Eliminating stagnant standing water and covering water containers
MCQ 3. When is the Aedes mosquito most active in biting humans?  • a. Midnight only  • b. Early morning (dawn) and late afternoon (dusk)  • c. Noon only  • d. During heavy rain
Ans: b. Early morning (dawn) and late afternoon (dusk)

MCQ 4. Why does only the female mosquito bite and suck human blood?  • a. She is hungrier  • b. She needs blood proteins to develop her eggs  • c. She has sharper wings  • d. Male mosquitoes cannot fly
Ans: b. She needs blood proteins to develop her eggs
Q1. Compare the transmission, vector, and symptoms of Malaria and Dengue fever.

Ans: Malaria is caused by the Plasmodium parasite transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito, characterized by high fever with shivering chills, sweating, and headache. Dengue is caused by a virus transmitted by the Aedes aegypti mosquito, characterized by sudden severe high fever, excruciating joint and muscle pain ('breakbone fever'), skin rash, retro-orbital pain behind the eyes, and dangerous platelet depletion.
Q2. Explain the life cycle of a mosquito and why targeting larvae is the most effective control strategy.

Ans: A mosquito undergoes four life stages: Egg, Larva, Pupa, and Adult. The first three stages occur exclusively in standing water. By eliminating stagnant water, introducing biological fish predators (Gambusia), or using larvicides, thousands of mosquitoes are eradicated before they ever develop wings to bite.
Q3. What personal and domestic precautions should families take to avoid mosquito-borne illnesses?

Ans: Families should install wire mesh screens on windows and doors, sleep under insecticide-treated bed nets, use mosquito repellent lotions, wear long-sleeved clothes, regularly empty and scrub water storage tubs, flowerpots, and air coolers, and ensure municipal fumigation is carried out.
Q4. What civic responsibilities do citizens share in preventing seasonal epidemics?

Ans: Citizens must avoid dumping trash into open street gutters, ensure proper disposal of used tires and plastic containers that trap rainwater, report stagnant sewage leaks to municipal authorities, and participate in community sanitation drives.
► 5.2 Speaking: Expressing Polite Satisfaction and Dissatisfaction on Civic Health Measures
► Polite Feedback on Municipal Vector Control Measures
Situation: Dialogue between a citizen and a Municipal Health Inspector regarding anti-dengue fumigation:
Citizen: Good morning, Inspector. While we are pleased with the regular trash collection this week, we are somewhat dissatisfied with the lack of anti-mosquito fogging in Sector 4.
Inspector: Good morning. I understand your concern and appreciate your polite feedback. Rainwater accumulated in vacant plots has increased the mosquito population.
Citizen: Could you kindly schedule a comprehensive fumigation drive in our street this Thursday evening?
Inspector: Certainly! I have scheduled our vector-control team to fumigate your entire sector tomorrow at 5:30 PM.
► 5.3 Language Practice: Simple & Compound Sentences and Reported Speech
■ EXERCISE 1: COMPOUND SENTENCES (USING COORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS) TABLE
Rainwater accumulated in the garden, so mosquitoes began breeding rapidly.
The patient had severe joint pain,
The patient had severe joint pain, but his platelet count remained stable.
You must sleep under a mosquito net,
You must sleep under a mosquito net, or you may contract malaria.
residents must still cover water tanks.
Fumigation was carried out yesterday, yet residents must still cover water tanks.
He used insect repellent lotion, and he wore protective long-sleeved clothing.
■ EXERCISE 2: DIRECT TO INDIRECT SPEECH (HEALTH WARNINGS) TABLE
The doctor said, "Do not allow water to stand in flowerpots."
The doctor advised us not to allow water to stand in flowerpots.
The health officer said, "Dengue larvae breed in clean standing water."
The health officer stated that dengue larvae breed in clean standing water.
Ali said to his brother, "Take the prescribed medicine on time."
Ali instructed his brother to take the prescribed medicine on time.
► 5.4 Writing: A Comprehensive Descriptive Essay on 'Combating Dengue and Malaria'
• Descriptive Essay: Combating Dengue and Malaria

Vector-borne infectious diseases, particularly Dengue fever and Malaria, pose recurring public health challenges in tropical and subtropical regions. Both diseases are transmitted through the bites of infected female mosquitoes—Anopheles in the case of Malaria, and Aedes aegypti in the case of Dengue. While Malaria causes cyclical fever with shivering chills, Dengue induces excruciating muscular aches, retro-orbital eye pain, and dangerous internal bleeding caused by severe platelet drop. Combating these diseases requires a multi-pronged strategy focused on vector eradication. At the household level, eliminating stagnant water from air coolers, roof drains, and plant saucers prevents larval development. At the civic level, timely municipal fumigation, covered sewerage lines, and widespread public health education are vital to protect our communities from seasonal epidemics.
► 5.5 Study Skills: Key Questions for a School Neighborhood Dengue Awareness Survey
Question 1: Are all domestic water storage tanks and drums tightly covered with lids in your household? (Yes / No)
Question 2: How frequently do you check and empty air cooler trays and flower pot saucers? (Daily / Weekly / Never)
Question 3: Has municipal anti-mosquito fumigation been conducted in your street in the past 30 days? (Yes / No)
Teaser 1. I am a striped mosquito that loves clean stagnant water and bites during daylight hours. Who am I?
Teaser 2. I am the microscopic parasite carried by the Anopheles mosquito that attacks red blood cells. Who am I?
Teaser 3. I am the fine protective mesh hung over beds that keeps nighttime pests away. Who am I?

content.text: THE MASTER SAHIB EDUCATIONAL SERIESCLASS IX ENGLISH — UNIT 6CIVIC SENSE & ROLE OF WOMEN(Complete Solved Textbook Exercises)
■  UNIT 6: CIVIC SENSE & ROLE OF WOMEN (SOLVED TEXTBOOK EXERCISES)
► 6.1 Reading Comprehension: The Role of Women in Pakistan's Creation and Development & The Daffodils (Poem by William Wordsworth)
Pre-Reading Q1. How did female leaders help shape the creation and survival of Pakistan during 1947?

Ans: Pioneering women like Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah and Begum Rana Liaquat Ali Khan mobilized millions of women, established refugee relief organizations, founded medical and educational institutions, and championed female political suffrage.
Pre-Reading Q2. How does the sight of natural beauty, like dancing daffodils, bring lasting tranquility to the human mind?

Ans: As William Wordsworth illustrated, experiencing the unblemished joy and beauty of nature creates enduring positive memories that rejuvenate the soul in moments of loneliness, pensive reflection, and stress.
■ VOCABULARY EXERCISE 2: CONTEXTUAL MEANINGS IN TEXTS TABLE
The foremost position in an army, social movement, or political struggle
The process of giving people social, political, or legal freedom and equal rights
A person who generously donates time and money to help the suffering and needy
The constitutional right to vote in national and local elections
Moving gently and quickly through the air in the breeze
The state or situation of being alone in peaceful contemplation
The human imagination and the memory of the mind
Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah was given the revered title of 'Madar-e-Millat' (Mother of the Nation).
Begum Rana Liaquat Ali Khan founded the All Pakistan Women's Association (APWA) in 1949.
In 'The Daffodils', the poet felt depressed and sorrowful in the company of the flowers.
False (F) — The poet felt immense, overflowing joy ('a poet could not but be gay in such a jocund company').
Pakistani women serve with distinction in the Armed Forces, civil bureaucracy, and corporate boardrooms.
Wordsworth compares the continuous stretch of daffodils to the stars that shine in the Milky Way.
MCQ 1. Which pioneer founded the All Pakistan Women's Association (APWA) to rehabilitate refugees?  • a. Bilquis Edhi  • b. Begum Rana Liaquat Ali Khan  • c. Lady Haroon  • d. Arfa Karim
Ans: b. Begum Rana Liaquat Ali Khan
MCQ 2. What poetic device is used in the line 'Ten thousand saw I at a glance'?  • a. Personification  • b. Hyperbole (deliberate poetic exaggeration)  • c. Simile  • d. Alliteration

MCQ 3. What does Wordsworth's 'inward eye' refer to in the final stanza of 'The Daffodils'?  • a. Medical eye drops  • b. The memory, imagination, and inner spiritual consciousness  • c. Sunglasses  • d. Reading glasses
Ans: b. The memory, imagination, and inner spiritual consciousness

MCQ 4. Who was the first woman in Asia to represent her country at the United Nations General Assembly in 1945?  • a. Begum Jahanara Shahnawaz  • b. Begum Shaista Ikramullah  • c. Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah  • d. Begum Salma Tassaduq Hussain
Q1. Describe the historic political and social contributions of Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah.

Ans: Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Quaid-e-Azam during the arduous struggle for Pakistan, established the Women's Relief Committee to assist millions of displaced 1947 refugees, advocated fiercely for constitutional democracy, and founded educational institutions for girls.
Q2. What were the foundational objectives of the All Pakistan Women's Association (APWA)?

Ans: Founded in 1949 by Begum Rana Liaquat Ali Khan, APWA aimed to advance women's legal rights, establish vocational training centres, build girls' schools and colleges, provide emergency refugee healthcare, and empower women to participate actively in socioeconomic nation building.
Q3. Explain the visual imagery and personification used in William Wordsworth's 'The Daffodils'.

Ans: Wordsworth personifies the golden daffodils as human dancers, describing them as 'fluttering and dancing in the breeze' and 'tossing their heads in sprightly dance'. He compares their golden density to the stars of the Milky Way, creating an enchanting scene of natural vitality.
Q4. How does the concluding stanza of 'The Daffodils' demonstrate the lasting power of poetry and nature?

Ans: The poet explains that whenever he lies on his couch in a vacant or pensive mood, the memory of the daffodils flashes upon his 'inward eye' (the bliss of solitude). Instantly, his heart fills with profound joy and dances alongside the flowers, illustrating how nature permanently heals the human spirit.
► 6.2 Speaking: Expressing Preferences and Constructive Opinions
► Expressing Preferences for Literary & Civic Studies
Situation: Discussion between students discussing preferences for literary study and social activism:
Ayesha: Do you prefer reading romantic nature poetry like Wordsworth's or historical biographies of national heroes?
Zoya: I find both valuable, but I personally prefer biographical accounts of leaders like Fatima Jinnah because they provide tangible real-life models of civic courage.
Ayesha: That is true; however, nature poetry like 'The Daffodils' teaches us observation, serenity, and artistic sensitivity, which balance our busy modern lives.
Zoya: A very perceptive point! Literature enriches our aesthetic sensibilities while history guides our civic duty.
► 6.3 Language Practice: Synonyms and Use of 'Since' vs 'For'
Refers to a specific starting point in time (e.g. 1947, 8:00 AM, Monday)
Pakistani women have contributed to national progress since 1947.
She has been studying Wordsworth's poetry since last week.
Refers to a duration / span of time (e.g. 10 years, 3 hours, 2 months)
APWA has been empowering underprivileged women for over seven decades.
The volunteers worked tirelessly in the relief camp for five days.
The children spent a jocund afternoon by the lake.
The students cheered with boundless glee upon winning the debate.
He sat in a pensive mood gazing at the starry night.
In vacant moments, beautiful memories bring comfort.
The dancers moved with sprightly grace across the stage.
► 6.4 Writing: A Comprehensive Narrative Essay on 'Pioneering Women of Pakistan'
• Narrative Essay: Pioneering Women of Pakistan

The creation and development of Pakistan stand as historic testaments to the indomitable courage and leadership of its women. From the inception of the Pakistan Movement, visionary women recognized that national freedom was inextricably linked with female emancipation. Mohtarma Fatima Jinnah mobilized female students, organized national committees, and stood as a towering symbol of constitutional integrity throughout her life. Similarly, Begum Rana Liaquat Ali Khan stepped forward during the catastrophic refugee crisis of 1947, organizing medical corps, food distribution networks, and ultimately establishing APWA to institutionalize women's legal and economic rights. Their pioneering legacy continues to inspire generations of modern Pakistani women who excel as fighter pilots, surgeons, researchers, and global entrepreneurs, demonstrating that women are equal architects of our nation's destiny.
► 6.5 Study Skills: Converting Brainstormed Points into a Published Article
1. Headline Selection: Craft an attention-grabbing title (e.g., 'Educating Women: The Catalyst for Economic Revival').
2. The Hook Paragraph: Start with an evocative quote from Quaid-e-Azam or a striking statistical insight.
3. Thematic Elaboration: Develop each brainstormed bullet into a structured paragraph with topic sentences and supporting evidence.
4. Call to Action: Conclude by urging policy makers and communities to guarantee equal opportunities.
► 6.6 Fun: Identifying Poetic Devices in 'The Daffodils'
Simile: 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' — Comparing the poet's wandering to a solitary cloud using 'as'.
Personification: 'Tossing their heads in sprightly dance' — Giving human dancing qualities to flowers.
Hyperbole: 'Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way' — Poetic exaggeration of numbers.
Metaphor: 'They flash upon that inward eye' — Describing spiritual memory as an inner eye.

content.text: THE MASTER SAHIB EDUCATIONAL SERIESCLASS IX ENGLISH — UNIT 7LIFE SKILLS(Complete Solved Textbook Exercises)
► 7.1 Reading Comprehension: The Secret of Success (The Hermit's Wisdom)
Pre-Reading Q1. What do you think is the true secret of lasting happiness and success in life?

Ans: The true secret of success lies in focusing entirely on the present moment, treating every person you interact with with kindness and empathy, and performing good deeds without selfish expectations.
Pre-Reading Q2. What three fundamental life questions did the wise King/Emperor seek to answer?
Ans: 1. What is the most important time to begin an action? 2. Who is the most important person to listen to? 3. What is the most important thing to do at all times?
■ VOCABULARY EXERCISE 2: CONTEXTUAL MEANINGS IN PARABLE TABLE
A person living in solitary seclusion for religious and spiritual meditation
An enemy, opponent, or rival in a dispute or conflict
A surprise attack made from a concealed position
Bound and dressed a physical wound with clean cloth to stop bleeding
Restored friendly and peaceful relations after a bitter feud
A tool with a broad metal blade used for digging ground
The state of being private and away from society
Deep sympathetic pity and concern for the misfortunes of others
The King went to meet the hermit dressed in royal robes with his army.
False (F) — The King dressed in simple peasant clothes and left his horse and guards behind.
The hermit was digging ground in front of his hut when the King arrived.
The King saved the life of a wounded man who had come to kill him.
The wounded man refused to forgive the King.
False (F) — The man was deeply touched by the King's care and swore lifelong loyalty to him.
The most important time in life is 'NOW' (the present moment).
MCQ 1. According to the hermit, what is the single most important time for every human being?  • a. Yesterday  • b. The Present Moment (NOW)  • c. Tomorrow morning  • d. Next year

MCQ 2. Who is the most important person in our lives according to the story's moral?  • a. A wealthy merchant  • b. The person you are with right at the present moment  • c. Someone far away  • d. A famous politician
Ans: b. The person you are with right at the present moment
MCQ 3. What is the most important business/work of human life?  • a. Accumulating gold  • b. Doing good and being kind to the person you are with  • c. Winning battles  • d. Building palaces
Ans: b. Doing good and being kind to the person you are with

MCQ 4. Why did the wounded man seek to kill the King initially?  • a. He was a foreign spy  • b. The King had executed his brother in war and seized his property  • c. He wanted the King's crown  • d. He was paid by bandits
Ans: b. The King had executed his brother in war and seized his property
Q1. What were the three questions that troubled the King, and why did he seek their answers?

Ans: The King believed that if he always knew: 1. The right time to begin any action, 2. The right people to consult, and 3. The most important thing to do, he would never fail in any undertaking. Finding scholars' answers conflicting, he sought the counsel of a renowned hermit.
Q2. How did the King save the life of his enemy without knowing his identity?

Ans: When a bearded man stumbled out of the woods bleeding profusely from a severe stomach wound, the King washed the wound, bound it with his handkerchief and the hermit's towel, and continually bathed it until the bleeding stopped. He then carried him into the hut and gave him fresh water.
Q3. How did the hermit explain the answers to the King's three questions through the day's events?

Ans: The hermit explained:1. If the King had not pitied the hermit's weakness and dug the beds, he would have been ambushed and killed. Thus, the most important time was when he was digging; the hermit was the most important man; and doing him good was his most important business.2. Later, the most important time was when he was nursing the wounded man, because otherwise the man would have died without making peace.3. Therefore, the only important time is NOW, because it is the only time we possess power. The most important person is the one you are with, and the most important pursuit is doing good.
Q4. What profound life skill does this parable teach regarding living mindfully?

Ans: It teaches that worrying over the uncontrollable past or unpredictable future causes anxiety. Living mindfully in the present moment, treating every human being with compassion, and taking immediate moral action represents the true essence of wisdom and success.
► 7.2 Speaking: Demonstrating the Conventions of Public Speaking
► Mindfulness and Compassion as Core Life Skills
Situation: Student presentation on 'Mindfulness and Compassion as Core Life Skills':
Speaker (Ali): Respected teachers and fellow students, imagine if every decision we made was rooted in empathy for the person standing right before us.
Audience Member: How can we practice this when life moves so fast?

Speaker (Ali): By remembering the hermit's rule: Focus your complete energy on the present task, listen actively to the person with you, and always choose kindness over anger. This simple mindfulness eliminates regret and builds lasting trust.
► 7.3 Language Practice: Advanced Voice Practice and Prefixes (re-, pre-, sub-, post-)
■ EXERCISE 1: ACTIVE TO PASSIVE VOICE TRANSFORMATION TABLE
The King bandaged the bleeding wound carefully.
The bleeding wound was bandaged carefully by the King.
The hermit was digging the ground with a spade.
The ground was being dug with a spade by the hermit.
The enemy has asked the King for forgiveness.
The King has been asked for forgiveness by the enemy.
We should always do good to our fellow human beings.
Good should always be done to our fellow human beings by us.
Wisdom solves the most complicated disputes.
The most complicated disputes are solved by wisdom.
■ EXERCISE 2: PREFIXES (RE-, PRE-, SUB-, POST-) TABLE
The King reconciled with his former adversary.
Our moral choices are not predetermined.
Treat every subordinate with justice and respect.
Post-war reconstruction brought peace to the region.
► 7.4 Writing: Compare and Contrast Essay on 'Material Wealth vs Spiritual Wisdom'
• Compare & Contrast Essay: Material Wealth vs Spiritual Wisdom

Throughout human history, individuals have sought success through two contrasting paths: the pursuit of material wealth and the cultivation of spiritual wisdom. Material success provides physical comfort, societal influence, and technological luxury; however, it often breeds anxiety, greed, and fear of loss when unaccompanied by ethical principles. In sharp contrast, spiritual wisdom, as demonstrated by the hermit in 'The Secret of Success', nurtures contentment, inner peace, and unconditional empathy for others. While material possessions are fleeting and perish with time, the enduring legacy of a wise and compassionate character enriches society across generations. True fulfillment is achieved when material resources are guided by moral wisdom to serve humanity.
► 7.5 Study Skills: Blueprint for Writing a Compelling Moral Parable
1. The Dilemma: Introduce a central philosophical question or ethical dilemma faced by the protagonist.
2. The Unfolding Trial: Create an unexpected encounter (such as a wounded stranger) that tests the protagonist's values.
3. The Revelation: Conclude with a wise mentor elucidating how practical compassion resolved the dilemma.
Ans: Odd One: Emperor (The others live in spiritual solitude).
Ans: Odd One: Arrogance (Negative vice, while others are virtues).

■  UNIT 8: PEOPLE AND PLACES (SOLVED TEXTBOOK EXERCISES)
► 8.1 Reading Comprehension: Ghazi's Diary & Abou Ben Adhem (Poem by Leigh Hunt)
■ PRE-READING QUESTIONS & LOVE FOR HUMANITY DISCUSSION
Pre-Reading Q1. Why is keeping a travel diary an enriching personal and literary habit?
Ans: A travel diary records vivid firsthand observations, geographic landscapes, unique cultural traditions, and emotional insights, turning personal journeys into lasting knowledge.
Pre-Reading Q2. What does the classic poem 'Abou Ben Adhem' teach about the connection between loving God and loving humanity?
Ans: It teaches that the highest form of worship and the surest way to earn God's divine love and blessings (benison) is to sincerely love, serve, and care for our fellow human beings.
■ VOCABULARY EXERCISE 2: CONTEXTUAL MEANINGS IN UNIT TABLE
A person who regularly writes personal thoughts, travels, and events in a diary
A slowly moving mass or river of ice formed by snow accumulation on mountains
Relating to high mountain regions and cold, elevated terrains
Went beyond what was expected in beauty, scale, or grandeur
A divine blessing, grace, or prayer of peace
Archaic poetic form for 'write' (referring to the angel's golden book)
A divine or supernatural apparition seen in a dream or waking state
Ghazi recorded his travels across the magnificent valleys of Hunza and Skardu in his diary.
In 'Abou Ben Adhem', the angel was writing in a book of gold in Abou's peaceful room.
Abou Ben Adhem's name appeared first in the initial list of those who love the Lord.
False (F) — Abou's name was not on the first list; he humbly asked to be written as one who loves his fellow men.
The next night, the angel revealed that Abou Ben Adhem's name led all the rest.
Robert Frost's famous line 'And miles to go before I sleep' symbolizes human duties and life's responsibilities before death.
MCQ 1. Who is the author of the beloved moral poem 'Abou Ben Adhem'?  • a. William Wordsworth  • b. Leigh Hunt  • c. Elsa Kazi  • d. Robert Frost

MCQ 2. What was the angel in Abou's room writing in the book of gold?  • a. The names of wealthy kings  • b. The names of those who love the Lord  • c. The names of great conquerors  • d. Mathematical formulas
Ans: b. The names of those who love the Lord

MCQ 3. What did Abou Ben Adhem humbly request the angel to write?  • a. Write me as a great warrior  • b. Write me as one that loves his fellow men  • c. Write me as a rich prince  • d. Do not write my name
Ans: b. Write me as one that loves his fellow men

MCQ 4. What did the angel reveal on the second night?  • a. The book was empty  • b. Abou's name led all the rest whom love of God had blessed  • c. Abou had failed  • d. The angel had vanished forever
Ans: b. Abou's name led all the rest whom love of God had blessed
Q1. Describe the celestial scene in Abou Ben Adhem's room when he awoke from a deep dream of peace.
Ans: Abou awoke to find his room bathed in serene moonlight, made extraordinarily rich and bright like a blooming lily by the presence of an angel writing in a golden book.
Q2. What profound spiritual truth does Leigh Hunt convey in 'Abou Ben Adhem'?

Ans: The poet conveys that God is pleased most not with ostentatious rituals or empty claims of piety, but with genuine, compassionate service to fellow human beings. Love for humanity is the true metric of divine favor.
Q3. What scenic highlights did Ghazi document in his northern Pakistan travel diary?

Ans: Ghazi documented the towering snow peaks of Rakaposhi and K2, the emerald waters of Lake Attabad, the ancient Baltit and Altit forts, massive sliding glaciers, and the warm hospitality and cultural resilience of northern communities.
Q4. Explain the metaphorical significance of Robert Frost's lines: 'The woods are lovely, dark and deep, / But I have promises to keep, / And miles to go before I sleep.'

Ans: The lovely woods represent the seductive beauty, rest, and peaceful withdrawal from worldly stress; however, the traveler cannot linger because he has moral promises, duties, and responsibilities to fulfill before the final sleep of death.
► 8.2 Speaking: Formal Debate on 'Ecotourism vs Industrial Commercialization'
► Formal Parliamentary Debate: Ecotourism vs Commercialization
Situation: Inter-class debate on preserving Pakistan's pristine northern ecology:
Proposition (Faraz): Mr. Speaker, rapid tourist hotel construction brings immediate revenue, road infrastructure, and local employment to remote mountain valleys.

Opposition (Saad): Mr. Speaker, unregulated commercial construction destroys fragile glacial ecosystems, causes landslides, and deforests native alpine valleys. We must enforce strict sustainable ecotourism to protect our natural heritage.
► 8.3 Language Practice: Degrees of Adverbs, Suffixes, and Direct Quotation Marks
■ EXERCISE 1: DEGREES OF COMPARISON FOR ADVERBS TABLE
The mountain jeep traveled fastest on the paved expressway.
The angel wrote most carefully in the book of gold.
Abou spoke more cheerfully upon hearing the angel.
Ghazi documented the mountain trail most clearly in his diary.
The hikers arrived later than expected due to snow.
Rule: Enclose exact spoken words within inverted commas (","); place the comma before the closing quotation mark.
Example 1: Abou spoke more low, "I pray thee, then, write me as one that loves his fellow men."
Example 2: Ghazi wrote in his diary, "The sunrise over Rakaposhi took our breath away."
► 8.4 Writing: A Comprehensive Critical Summary of Leigh Hunt's 'Abou Ben Adhem'
• Critical Summary: Abou Ben Adhem (by Leigh Hunt)

Leigh Hunt's classic poem 'Abou Ben Adhem' is an inspiring moral narrative celebrating universal love for humanity as the supreme path to divine grace. The poem opens with Abou ben Adhem awakening from a peaceful dream to witness a radiant angel writing in a book of gold. When Abou inquires about the text, the angel informs him that it lists those who love God. Discovering that his name is absent, Abou remains untroubled and humbly requests: 'Write me as one that loves his fellow men.' The following night, the angel reappears in blinding celestial light to reveal the names of those blessed by God's love, and lo! Abou ben Adhem's name leads all the rest. Through simple, melodious rhyming couplets, the poem immortalizes the golden truth that true spirituality is measured through selfless love and service to our fellow human beings.
► 8.5 Study Skills: Presentation Delivery Evaluation Rubric
Content & Structure (30%): Clear introduction, logical arguments, and a memorable concluding summary.
Vocal Delivery (30%): Audible projection, expressive intonation, and effective pausing.
Body Language (20%): Confident posture, natural gestures, and continuous eye contact with the entire audience.
Time Management (20%): Completing all presentation sections within the allotted 5-minute time frame.
► 8.6 Fun: Dramatic Recitation of Abou Ben Adhem's Climax
"The angel wrote, and vanished. The next night
It came again with a great wakening light,
And showed the names whom love of God had blest,
And lo! Ben Adhem's name led all the rest!"

- Ask students to finish the project at home if needed. Remind them to bring it to class the next day.

- Review key points from the unit using flashcards or a short quiz game.
- Students present their projects to the class. Each group will take turns explaining their project.
- Q&A session about the projects. Encourage students to ask questions and provide positive feedback.
- Reflect on what was learned during the unit. Ask students to share their favorite part and what they found most interesting.
- Provide a review worksheet to summarize the unit. This could include questions about the key points covered.
- Ask students to write a reflection on what they learned and enjoyed the most during the unit.

content.text: Daily Lesson Plan for Grade 1 English
Dates: September 15 - September 22Theme: Introduction to Letters and Phonetic Sounds
Day 1: 15th September (Friday) - Introduction to Letters A-E
Objective: Recognize and pronounce letters A-E; associate them with their sounds.
Islamic Integration: Discuss the importance of learning to read, as inspired by the first revelation of the Quran (“Iqra” - Read).
Materials: Alphabet chart, flashcards, markers, worksheets.
Start by singing the ABC song together.
Show a colourful alphabet chart, pointing to A-E while students repeat.
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Recognize and Pronounce Letters
Use flashcards to show letters A-E individually.
Ask students to repeat each letter and make the corresponding sound (e.g., “A is for apple, ‘a’ sound”).
Encourage students to identify letters on their desks or in the room (e.g., A on a poster).
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Match Letters with Objects
Show images (apple, egg, ice cream, etc.) and ask students to match the images with the correct letters.
Pair students to discuss other objects that start with A-E.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): ABC Sound Game
Use a tablet or computer to play an interactive ABC sound game where students hear the sound and see the letter.
Review the letters A-E and discuss why learning letters is important for reading.
Students complete a worksheet where they trace and color letters A-E.
Draw three objects that start with A, B, or C and label them.
Teacher assesses students' engagement and pronunciation accuracy.
Objective: Recognize and pronounce letters F-J; associate them with their sounds.
Islamic Integration: Relate the ability to learn and communicate to Allah’s gift of knowledge.
Recap letters A-E from the previous lesson.
Introduce today’s focus (F-J) using a song or chant.
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Sound and Letter Recognition
Show flashcards for F-J, and ask students to say each letter and sound (e.g., “F is for fish”).
Encourage students to form the letters with their hands or using letter blocks.
Organize a mini scavenger hunt in the classroom where students find objects or pictures that start with F-J.
Play a short phonics game focusing on letters F-J using a tablet.
Discuss which letters were the easiest and which were more challenging.
Complete a tracing and matching worksheet for F-J.
Practice writing F-J in the notebook three times.
Note which students were able to connect sounds with letters accurately.
Objective: Recognize and pronounce letters K-O; associate them with their sounds.
Islamic Integration: Discuss the use of writing and reading in daily life, including reading the Quran.
Materials: Alphabet strips, flashcards, whiteboard, markers.
Quick recap of F-J with flashcards.
Introduce letters K-O with a fun rhyme or chant.
Demonstrate writing K-O on the board and have students practice on their individual whiteboards.
Emphasize correct formation of each letter.
Students match flashcards with objects or pictures (e.g., K for kite, O for octopus).
Encourage students to say the sound aloud.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Interactive Alphabet Song
Use a digital resource to play an interactive alphabet song focusing on K-O.
Discuss how many objects they know that start with these letters.
Write sentences using words that start with K-O (e.g., “The kite is blue.”).
Find pictures in a magazine or newspaper of things starting with K-O.
Assess which letters were most recognized and where reinforcement is needed.
Objective: Recognize and pronounce letters P-T; associate them with their sounds.
Islamic Integration: Reflect on how learning helps us understand and follow good teachings.
Introduce P-T using a storytelling method (e.g., “Once there was a panda who loved tea.”).
Use letter blocks to form words starting with P-T.
Students work in pairs to create as many words as possible.
Draw objects that start with P-T and label them.
Watch a short video focused on letter sounds P-T.
Discuss which letters were most fun to learn and why.
Worksheet on tracing and matching words starting with P-T.
Write three sentences using words that start with P, Q, R, S, or T.
Teacher notes areas of improvement needed for specific students.
Objective: Recognize and pronounce letters U-Z; associate them with their sounds.
Islamic Integration: Relate learning letters to reading texts like the Quran and daily Duas.
Recap P-T using a quick review game.
Introduce U-Z with a fun chant.
Use flashcards and repeat the sounds of U-Z.
Students repeat and identify the beginning sound of each word.
Students draw and color the objects.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Sound Matching Game
Play a game matching sounds to letters U-Z.
Discuss favorite new words learned from U-Z.
Practice writing U-Z and draw an animal or object starting with these letters.
Evaluate the effectiveness of sound recognition and participation.
Day 6: 22nd September (Friday) - Review of All Letters (A-Z)
Objective: Review and reinforce recognition of all letters A-Z.
Islamic Integration: Emphasize the importance of learning and reading in Islam.
Materials: Complete set of flashcards, board, worksheets.
Recap all letters A-Z using a sing-along.
Play a bingo game where students mark off letters as they hear the sounds.
Quick-fire questions using flashcards, where students say the sound and a word for each letter.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Interactive Alphabet Review
Use a tablet to play a full alphabet review game.
Reflect on which letters were easiest and which were the hardest.
Complete a comprehensive worksheet covering all letters.
Revise any letters that were challenging and practice with parents.
Reflect on overall progress; identify students who need additional support.
Objective: Understand the concept of describing words (adjectives) and use them in sentences.
Islamic Integration: Use adjectives to describe Allah’s creations, emphasizing the beauty and variety found in nature.
Materials: Picture cards, drawing sheets, markers, whiteboard.
Show students a beautiful picture of nature (mountains, rivers, etc.) and ask them to describe what they see (e.g., green trees, tall mountains).
Introduce the concept of adjectives as words that describe things.
Display picture cards with different objects (e.g., a big elephant, a small kitten, a red apple).
Ask students to describe the objects using appropriate adjectives. Write these on the board.
Let students look around the classroom to find objects they can describe (e.g., blue bag, tall chair).
Students take turns sharing their descriptions with the class.
Show a short-animated video that explains adjectives and provides examples in a fun way.
Discuss why adjectives are important in making sentences more interesting and detailed.
Worksheet where students match objects with suitable adjectives (e.g., matching a picture of a sun with “hot” or “bright”).
At home, find three objects and write two adjectives for each (e.g., “soft pillow,” “cold water”).
Teacher evaluates students’ participation and understanding of using adjectives in everyday descriptions.
Objective: Use adjectives to describe elements of nature.
Islamic Integration: Highlight Allah’s creation in nature using adjectives (e.g., vast ocean, beautiful flowers).
Materials: Nature posters, drawing sheets, crayons.
Show posters of nature scenes and ask, “What do you see? How would you describe it?”
Write students’ responses on the board and underline the adjectives.
Give students drawing sheets and ask them to draw a scene from nature (e.g., a garden, beach).
After drawing, they label their drawing with descriptive words (e.g., blue sky, green grass).
Students share their drawings and descriptions with the class.
Encourage them to use more adjectives to make their descriptions vivid.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Interactive Nature Scene
Use an educational app to explore a digital nature scene, identifying and describing elements using adjectives.
Discuss the variety and beauty in nature and how adjectives help us appreciate it.
Complete a worksheet where they fill in the blanks with appropriate adjectives (e.g., “The ____ flower,” “The ____ ocean”).
Find one nature picture at home and write three sentences describing it using adjectives.
Assess how well students are incorporating adjectives into their descriptions and sentences.
Objective: Use adjectives to describe people’s appearance and personality.
Islamic Integration: Use positive adjectives to describe good character traits promoted in Islam, such as kind, honest, and helpful.
Materials: Pictures of different people, whiteboard, markers.
Show pictures of different people (children, adults, characters) and ask, “How would you describe this person?”
Introduce adjectives related to appearance (e.g., tall, short) and personality (e.g., happy, kind).
Use images or draw simple characters on the board.
Encourage students to describe each character using two adjectives.
Pair up students and have them describe each other using kind adjectives.
Share with the class and focus on positive words.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Descriptive Adjectives Game
Play a game where students match adjectives to people shown in an interactive video.
Discuss how words can make people feel happy when used positively.
Worksheet: Students draw themselves and write three adjectives that describe their appearance and personality.
At home, describe a family member using three positive adjectives.
Reflect on students’ understanding of using adjectives to describe people and their awareness of positive words.
Objective: Identify and use adjectives to describe everyday objects.
Islamic Integration: Encourage gratitude for the objects we have and describe them positively.
Materials: Everyday classroom objects, picture cards, whiteboard.
Show a common object (e.g., a book, a pencil) and ask students, “What words can we use to describe this?”
Write responses on the board, emphasizing adjectives.
Divide the class into small groups, each with a set of objects (e.g., ball, cup, bag).
Students describe each object and share with the class.
Display picture cards of various objects and ask students to match adjectives (e.g., a “red” ball, a “soft” pillow).
Use an online interactive quiz to identify adjectives for different objects shown on the screen.
Talk about why describing objects can help us communicate better.
Complete a worksheet that has objects needing matching adjectives.
Describe three objects at home and use one adjective for each.
Evaluate students’ descriptions and their engagement in identifying adjectives for objects.
Objective: Review and reinforce understanding of adjectives through various activities.
Islamic Integration: Reflect on the importance of using words wisely, including kind adjectives to describe people and things.
Materials: All previous worksheets, flashcards, drawing sheets.
Quick recap game: Call out objects, people, or scenes, and ask students to respond with an adjective.
Play a bingo game where students have to match descriptions with pictures on their bingo cards.
In groups, students are given a picture scene and asked to come up with as many adjectives as possible.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Adjectives Match-Up
Use a digital matching game that reinforces adjective identification.
Discuss the most interesting adjectives learned and how they can be used in writing.
Complete a review worksheet that includes fill-in-the-blanks, matching, and short descriptions.
Write a short paragraph describing your favourite place using at least five adjectives.
Reflect on the week’s learning and identify areas that need reinforcement.
Week 3: Writing Patterns and Forming Words
Dates: October 2 - October 6Theme: Learning to write using patterns and forming simple words
Day 12: 2nd October (Monday) - Writing Patterns (Straight Lines and Curves)
Objective: Practice writing straight lines and curves as foundational skills for letter formation.
Islamic Integration: Relate neat writing and practice to discipline and patience, values emphasized in Islam.
Materials: Writing worksheets, whiteboards, markers, pencils.
Begin with a brief discussion on why writing neatly is important, connecting it to reading and understanding religious texts like the Quran.
Show examples of straight lines and curves on the board.
Demonstrate how to draw straight lines and curves on the board.
Provide students with whiteboards to practice drawing straight lines first, then curves, mimicking the teacher’s demonstration.
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Line and Curve Tracing
Distribute worksheets with tracing lines and curves.
Encourage students to trace slowly and carefully, focusing on accuracy and control.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Interactive Tracing Game
Use a digital resource (tablet or laptop) to allow students to trace lines and curves on-screen, reinforcing the skill in an engaging format.
Discuss which patterns were easier or harder and why practice is important.
Complete a worksheet where students trace straight lines and curves, then draw their own.
Practice drawing straight lines and curves in a notebook at home.
Reflect on students’ ability to follow the patterns and identify those needing extra support.
Day 13: 3rd October (Tuesday) - Zigzag Patterns and Simple Words
Objective: Practice zigzag patterns and begin forming simple words using learned patterns.
Islamic Integration: Relate the effort in writing to putting in effort in daily good deeds.
Materials: Zigzag pattern sheets, markers, pencils.
Show examples of zigzag patterns and discuss where they can be seen in the real world (e.g., lightning, design patterns).
Draw zigzags on the board and encourage students to try in the air with their fingers.
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Zigzag Tracing and Drawing
Guide students as they trace, then draw their zigzag lines, emphasizing accuracy.
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Forming Words Using Zigzag Patterns
Use zigzag patterns to form simple words like "cat" and "bat," focusing on the zigzag pattern in the letters (e.g., “t” in “bat”).
Practice writing these words on the board.
Use an educational app to trace zigzag patterns interactively.
Discuss why learning these patterns helps in writing letters and words.
Complete worksheets with additional zigzag patterns and simple words.
Trace and draw zigzag patterns at home, and try writing “cat” and “bat.”
Teacher notes students’ control in drawing zigzags and writing related words.
Day 14: 4th October (Wednesday) - Circular Patterns and Word Formation
Objective: Practice circular writing patterns; integrate into forming letters and simple words.
Islamic Integration: Discuss circular shapes in nature and Islamic art (e.g., circles in mosque designs).
Materials: Circular pattern worksheets, crayons, markers.
Show examples of circular patterns found in Islamic art and nature.
Ask students to identify circular objects around the classroom (e.g., clock, wheels).
Demonstrate how to draw smooth circles on the board.
Students practice on their whiteboards before moving to worksheets.
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Writing Circular Letters and Words
Practice writing letters that use circular patterns (e.g., "o," "c") and simple words like “dog,” “log.”
Students practice writing these words on their worksheets.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Circle Tracing Game
Use an app that reinforces circular tracing through interactive games.
Discuss how mastering circular shapes helps in writing neatly.
Complete a worksheet with circular patterns and words to trace and write.
Practice writing circles and try writing "dog" and "log" at home.
Teacher evaluates students’ control over circular writing and forming words.
Day 15: 5th October (Thursday) - Diagonal Patterns and Writing Words
Objective: Practice diagonal lines and integrate them into writing letters and simple words.
Islamic Integration: Discuss diagonal patterns seen in nature, such as branches of trees.
Materials: Diagonal pattern sheets, pencils, whiteboards.
Show images of diagonal patterns in nature and architecture.
Introduce diagonal patterns by drawing them on the board.
Students trace diagonal lines on their worksheets, practicing different angles.
Encourage them to try drawing without tracing once comfortable.
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Writing Diagonal Letters and Words
Focus on writing letters that use diagonal strokes (e.g., "v," "x") and simple words like “van,” “box.”
Practice these words on the board and in their notebooks.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Diagonal Tracing App
Use an interactive tracing app focusing on diagonal lines.
Reflect on how diagonal lines are part of many letters and their importance in writing.
Complete a worksheet with diagonal patterns and related words.
Practice writing diagonal lines and try writing “van” and “box.”
Assess students’ skill levels in maintaining neatness and control when writing diagonally.
Day 16: 6th October (Friday) - Review of Writing Patterns
Objective: Review all writing patterns and assess students’ ability to form letters and words.
Islamic Integration: Emphasize patience and practice, linking to perseverance in learning as taught in Islam.
Materials: Mixed pattern worksheets, board markers, student notebooks.
Quick review of all patterns learned (straight, zigzag, circular, diagonal).
Ask students to demonstrate their favorite pattern on the board.
Play a bingo game where students identify patterns called out by the teacher.
Students mark off matching patterns on their cards.
A fun challenge where students write as many words as they can using the patterns learned.
Display the best attempts on a “Writing Stars” board.
Use an online quiz that reviews all the patterns with interactive elements.
Discuss which patterns helped them write best and areas for improvement.
Complete a mixed worksheet that includes all patterns and words.
Practice at home with favorite patterns and write a few sentences using words learned.
Evaluate the students’ grasp of each pattern and plan to revisit any challenging areas.
Dates: October 9 - October 13Theme: Learning to form basic sentences using nouns, verbs, and adjectives.
Day 17: 9th October (Monday) - Forming Sentences with “This is...”
Objective: Form basic sentences using the structure “This is...”.
Islamic Integration: Use sentences like “This is a good deed” to relate learning to positive actions in Islam.
Materials: Sentence strips, picture cards, whiteboard, markers.
Start with a simple question: “What do we say when we see something new?”
Introduce the sentence structure “This is...” with examples on the board (e.g., “This is a book.”).
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Sentence Formation with Pictures
Display picture cards (e.g., apple, cat, book).
Ask students to create sentences using “This is...” for each picture.
Write the sentences on the board and have students repeat them.
Provide sentence strips with pictures and ask students to match and write the correct “This is...” sentence.
Encourage students to come up with their own sentences using classroom objects.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Interactive Sentence Builder
Use a digital resource where students drag and drop words to form “This is...” sentences.
Discuss how forming sentences helps in communication and reading.
Complete a worksheet with pictures and blank spaces to write “This is...” sentences.
Write three “This is...” sentences using objects at home (e.g., “This is a table.”).
Reflect on students’ abilities to form sentences independently and identify areas that need reinforcement.
Day 18: 10th October (Tuesday) - Forming Sentences with “I have...”
Objective: Form sentences using the structure “I have...”.
Islamic Integration: Use examples like “I have a kind heart” to encourage positive self-expression.
Begin by asking students what they have in their bags.
Write responses on the board using the structure “I have...” (e.g., “I have a pencil.”).
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Using Flashcards to Form Sentences
Show flashcards with objects and actions (e.g., ball, toy).
Students form sentences using “I have...” (e.g., “I have a ball.”).
Distribute sentence strips and pictures for students to match and read aloud.
Practice writing the sentences in their notebooks.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Sentence Formation Game
Use an app that allows students to construct sentences by selecting words.
Discuss how “I have...” can be used to describe belongings and feelings.
Worksheet with images where students write “I have...” sentences.
Write four “I have...” sentences about things they own or like.
Assess how confidently students can form sentences using this structure.
Day 19: 11th October (Wednesday) - Forming Sentences with “She is...” and “He is...”
Objective: Use “He is...” and “She is...” to describe people and actions.
Islamic Integration: Emphasize describing good character traits as seen in Islamic teachings.
Materials: Character flashcards, sentence boards, markers.
Show pictures of people and ask, “What can we say about them?”
Introduce the structures “He is...” and “She is...” on the board.
Use character flashcards to form sentences (e.g., “He is tall.”, “She is happy.”).
Write sentences on the board, and have students repeat.
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Matching Characters to Sentences
Students match characters with sentences using “He is...” or “She is...”.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Story with Sentences
Use a short animated story that highlights sentences using “He is...” and “She is...”.
Reflect on how we can describe others kindly and accurately.
Complete a worksheet that includes drawing characters and writing sentences about them.
Write two sentences using “He is...” and “She is...” about family members.
Observe how well students understand the use of gender-specific sentences.
Objective: Practice combining simple sentences to form more complex thoughts.
Islamic Integration: Encourage combining sentences to make stories that reflect good actions and values.
Begin with a storytelling session, showing how combining sentences creates a narrative.
Write simple sentences on the board and combine them (e.g., “This is a cat. It is cute.”).
Provide sentence cards and guide students on combining them to form more detailed sentences.
Write combinations on the board and read together.
In small groups, students work together to combine sentences and read aloud.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Interactive Sentence Combiner
Use an app that allows students to combine sentences digitally and see immediate results.
Discuss how combining sentences makes writing and speaking more interesting.
Complete a worksheet where students combine sentences provided.
Write a short paragraph using combined sentences about a favorite activity.
Teacher evaluates students’ abilities to combine sentences creatively.
Day 21: 13th October (Friday) - Review and Practice of Sentences
Objective: Review all sentence structures learned throughout the week.
Islamic Integration: Reflect on the power of words and sentences in sharing knowledge and kindness.
Materials: Sentence flashcards, student notebooks, board.
Quick recap using a question game: “Who can tell me a sentence with ‘This is...’?”
Engage students by asking for examples from the week.
Play Bingo with sentence strips, where students match sentence beginnings with correct endings.
A timed challenge where students build as many sentences as possible using given words.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Sentence Review Game
Use a game that tests students’ ability to recognize and form the sentences learned.
Discuss the favourite sentence structures and why they like using them.
Review worksheet with mixed sentences to form and complete.
Write a small story using at least five sentences learned this week.
Reflect on the week’s progress and identify students needing more practice.
Week 5: Vocabulary Building - Fruits and Vegetables
Dates: October 16 - October 20Theme: Learning the names, characteristics, and uses of fruits and vegetables.
Objective: Learn the names of common fruits and use descriptive words for them.
Islamic Integration: Discuss fruits mentioned in the Quran, such as dates, figs, and pomegranates, emphasizing gratitude for Allah’s blessings.
Materials: Real fruits (if available), picture cards of fruits, flashcards, drawing sheets, whiteboard.
Display a variety of fruits in the classroom (real or pictures).
Ask students to name the fruits they recognize and describe them (e.g., color, taste).
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Fruit Identification and Description
Show flashcards of different fruits (apple, banana, mango).
As each fruit is shown, students identify it and use one adjective to describe it (e.g., “yellow banana,” “sweet apple”).
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Drawing and Labeling Fruits
Students draw their favorite fruit and write its name and a descriptive word underneath.
Display the drawings around the classroom.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Interactive Fruit Game
Use an app or website where students match fruit names to pictures in a timed game.
Discuss the importance of fruits in a healthy diet and how they are used in daily life.
Complete a worksheet with pictures of fruits and blank spaces to write their names.
Find a fruit at home, draw it, and write a sentence about it (e.g., “This is an orange. It is round and juicy.”).
Reflect on students’ ability to identify fruits and use descriptive language.
Objective: Learn the names of common vegetables and describe them using adjectives.
Islamic Integration: Emphasize the significance of healthy eating as recommended in Islam and the variety Allah has created.
Materials: Real vegetables (if available), vegetable picture cards, flashcards, whiteboard.
Show a selection of vegetables (real or pictures) and ask students to name as many as they can.
Discuss why eating vegetables is good for health.
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Vegetable Identification and Description
Display picture cards of vegetables (e.g., carrot, cucumber, spinach).
Students identify each vegetable and describe it using adjectives (e.g., “green spinach,” “crunchy carrot”).
Students sort pictures into categories (leafy, root, seed vegetables) on the board.
Discuss the characteristics of each type.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Vegetable Matching Game
Use an interactive digital game to match vegetable names to their pictures.
Discuss the different ways vegetables can be cooked and eaten.
Worksheet with pictures of vegetables, where students label each one.
Draw a vegetable from home and write a sentence describing it (e.g., “This is a carrot. It is orange and crunchy.”).
Assess students’ understanding of vegetable vocabulary and descriptive language.
Day 24: 18th October (Wednesday) - Comparing Fruits and Vegetables
Objective: Understand the differences and similarities between fruits and vegetables.
Islamic Integration: Relate to the variety and blessings of food provided by Allah.
Materials: Venn diagram sheets, picture cards of fruits and vegetables, markers.
Begin with a discussion on what makes fruits and vegetables different.
Show examples and ask students to sort them verbally.
Draw a large Venn diagram on the board.
As a class, sort fruits and vegetables into their respective sections, discussing similarities (e.g., both can be eaten raw) and differences (e.g., fruits have seeds).
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Sorting and Group Activity
Students work in groups to sort picture cards into fruits and vegetables and place them in the correct sections of their Venn diagrams.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Fruits vs. Vegetables Quiz
Use an interactive quiz that asks students to identify whether a picture shows a fruit or vegetable.
Discuss why it’s important to eat both fruits and vegetables and how each benefits our health.
Complete a worksheet comparing fruits and vegetables using a Venn diagram format.
At home, identify two fruits and two vegetables, draw them, and write one similarity and one difference.
Evaluate students’ comprehension of the characteristics of fruits and vegetables.
Day 25: 19th October (Thursday) - Drawing and Labeling Fruits/Vegetables
Objective: Reinforce vocabulary by drawing and labeling fruits and vegetables.
Islamic Integration: Encourage creativity and reflect on the beauty of Allah’s creation in nature.
Materials: Drawing sheets, crayons, picture cards.
Discuss why fruits and vegetables are so colorful and unique.
Show examples and encourage students to think about how they would describe them.
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Drawing and Describing Fruits/Vegetables
Students choose a fruit and a vegetable to draw.
Label each drawing with its name and one descriptive word (e.g., “juicy watermelon,” “crisp lettuce”).
Students present their drawings to the class and describe their chosen fruit and vegetable.
Display drawings around the room as a “Garden of Words.”
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Drawing Game
Use a drawing app where students can draw and label fruits and vegetables digitally.
Reflect on the different colors, textures, and shapes found in nature.
Complete a worksheet where students draw and label another set of fruits and vegetables.
Find a fruit or vegetable not discussed in class, draw it, and label it with an adjective.
Teacher evaluates students’ ability to creatively express their understanding through art and writing.
Day 26: 20th October (Friday) - Vocabulary Review of Fruits and Vegetables
Objective: Review and reinforce the vocabulary of fruits and vegetables learned throughout the week.
Islamic Integration: Reflect on the importance of variety in our diet as part of a balanced and healthy lifestyle encouraged in Islam.
Materials: Flashcards, whiteboard, markers, drawing sheets.
Start with a quick game where students describe a fruit or vegetable without naming it, and the class guesses.
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Fruit and Vegetable Bingo
Play Bingo with fruit and vegetable names and pictures.
Students mark off the correct picture as the teacher calls out names.
Divide the class into groups. Each group takes turns naming a fruit or vegetable without repeating any previously mentioned.
The group with the most correct names wins.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Vocabulary Review Game
Use an interactive vocabulary review game that focuses on fruit and vegetable recognition.
Discuss how fruits and vegetables contribute to a healthy life.
Complete a review worksheet where students match pictures of fruits and vegetables with their names.
Write a short story or paragraph using at least five fruits or vegetables learned during the week.
Assess students’ recall of vocabulary and their ability to describe the items effectively.
Dates: October 23 - October 27Theme: Understanding and using singular and plural nouns correctly.
Day 27: 23rd October (Monday) - Understanding Singular and Plural
Objective: Differentiate between singular and plural forms of nouns.
Islamic Integration: Relate to the concept of gratitude and counting blessings in life, as taught in Islam.
Materials: Flashcards with singular and plural images, whiteboard, markers.
Start with a discussion: “What is the difference between one apple and many apples?”
Show a few objects (e.g., one book, two books) and ask students to identify how many.
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Singular and Plural Flashcards
Show flashcards with singular and plural pictures (e.g., one cat vs. two cats).
Introduce the concept of adding “s” or “es” to make things plural.
Provide students with picture cards of singular and plural objects.
Students sort them into “Singular” and “Plural” piles on their desks.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Singular and Plural Matching Game
Use an interactive game on a tablet or computer where students match singular words to their plural forms.
Discuss why we use singular and plural in everyday conversation.
Complete a worksheet where students write the plural form of each singular noun shown.
Find five singular objects at home and write their plural forms.
Assess students’ understanding of singular vs. plural and their engagement during activities.
Objective: Practice forming plurals by adding “s” to singular nouns.
Islamic Integration: Use examples that count blessings, like “one good deed” vs. “many good deeds.”
Materials: Flashcards, whiteboard, markers, picture cards.
Write a few singular words on the board and ask, “What happens when there’s more than one?”
Introduce the rule of adding “s” to make plurals.
Display objects or images (e.g., dog, car, pencil) and practice adding “s” to make them plural.
Write the words on the board together.
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Singular to Plural Card Matching
Distribute singular and plural cards to students.
Students find the matching pair (e.g., dog - dogs) and form sentences using them.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Plural Formation
Use an app that allows students to drag singular words into a plural formation activity.
Discuss when and why we use “s” to make plurals and when other endings might be needed.
Worksheet where students write plurals by adding “s” to given singular nouns.

Day 57: 4th December (Monday) - Final Projects and Presentations
Objective: Engage students in presenting their favorite learning projects from the term, reinforcing communication and presentation skills.
Islamic Integration: Encourage students to express gratitude for their learning experiences and to share knowledge with others.
Materials: Student projects, presentation sheets, markers, whiteboard.
Start with an inspirational message: “Sharing what we’ve learned helps others learn too!”
Explain that students will present their favorite project or topic from the term.
Each student presents their chosen project, whether it’s a drawing, a short story, or a favorite lesson.
Encourage students to speak confidently and use descriptive language.
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Peer Feedback and Appreciation
After each presentation, classmates give positive feedback (e.g., “I liked your drawing,” or “Your story was interesting”).
Reinforce the importance of supporting each other.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Presentation Showcase
Use a digital platform to display student projects (e.g., a slideshow of artwork or stories).
Reflect on what students enjoyed most about presenting and what they learned from each other.
Complete a reflection sheet on their presentation experience.
Discuss their presentation with family and share their favorite part of the project.
Reflect on students’ communication skills and their ability to express their learning journey.
Day 58: 5th December (Tuesday) - Classroom Cleanup and Organizing Materials
Objective: Organize classroom materials, review personal work, and prepare for the end of the term.
Islamic Integration: Highlight the importance of cleanliness and orderliness, which are valued in Islam.
Materials: Cleaning supplies, organization bins, personal folders.
Discuss why keeping our spaces clean and organized is important, linking it to respect for our learning environment.
Show how cleaning up can be a fun and rewarding activity.
Help students organize their work into personal folders, sorting by subjects or type of work.
Reflect on the progress shown in their work from the start of the term to the end.
Divide students into teams responsible for different tasks (e.g., cleaning desks, sorting books, organizing supplies).
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Declutter Game
Use a digital game that teaches the importance of organization and cleaning.
Reflect on how good organization can help make the classroom a more enjoyable place to learn.
Complete a checklist of tasks to ensure all areas are clean and organized.
Practice organizing a space at home, such as their room or study area.
Reflect on the value of keeping a clean and orderly environment.
Day 59: 6th December (Wednesday) - Reflective Art and Creative Writing
Objective: Use art and creative writing to reflect on the term’s experiences and express feelings about learning.
Islamic Integration: Encourage creativity as a way to appreciate and reflect on the blessings of knowledge.
Materials: Drawing paper, crayons, colored pencils, reflection prompts.
Discuss how art and writing can help us express what we’ve learned and how we feel.
Show examples of reflective art and encourage students to think creatively.
Provide prompts like “Draw your favorite moment from the term” or “Draw what makes you happy in school.”
Encourage students to add words or sentences to their drawings.
Students write a short paragraph about their favorite memory or what they learned that was most meaningful.
Share their writing in small groups.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Drawing and Writing Tool
Use an app that allows students to create digital drawings or write stories.
Discuss how expressing our thoughts through art and writing helps us remember and appreciate our experiences.
Complete their drawing and writing, then display on a classroom “Memory Wall.”
Share their art and writing with a family member and talk about what they drew or wrote.
Reflect on students’ ability to express their feelings and experiences through creative outlets.
Day 60: 7th December (Thursday) - Thank You Cards and Letters
Objective: Create thank you cards or letters to express gratitude to teachers, classmates, or family members.
Islamic Integration: Emphasize gratitude as a key Islamic value, showing appreciation to those who help us learn.
Materials: Cardstock, colored pencils, stickers, markers.
Discuss the importance of saying “thank you” and recognizing those who support us.
Highlight how showing gratitude makes others feel appreciated.
Activity 1 (15 minutes): Making Thank You Cards
Provide materials for students to create thank you cards for someone special (e.g., a teacher, parent, or friend).
Activity 2 (10 minutes): Writing Thank You Letters
Students write a short letter of thanks, focusing on specific actions or support they received.
Share letters with the class if comfortable.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Digital Card Making
Use a digital tool that allows students to design and print thank you cards.
Reflect on how it feels to give and receive thanks, and why gratitude is important.
Complete their thank you cards and letters, then place them in envelopes to deliver.
Give their thank you cards or letters to the intended person and observe the reaction.
Reflect on the impact of expressing gratitude and how it strengthens relationships.
Day 61: 8th December (Friday) - Farewell Party and Class Celebration
Objective: Celebrate the end of the term with a fun farewell party, reflecting on achievements and enjoying the last day together.
Islamic Integration: Encourage thankfulness for the time spent learning and growing together.
Welcome students to the celebration, expressing pride in their achievements.
Set the tone for a fun and joyful day.
Play fun, inclusive games that everyone can enjoy (e.g., musical chairs, guessing games).
Use music to create a joyful atmosphere.
Present certificates to each student, highlighting their unique strengths and contributions.
ICT Activity (5 minutes): Slideshow of Memories
Show a digital slideshow of photos and highlights from the term, capturing special moments.
Reflect on the term, share favourite memories, and discuss what they are looking forward to next.
None—focus on celebrating and enjoying the moment.
Share the celebration with family and talk about their favourite part of the day.
Reflect on the students’ growth and celebrate the community built within the classroom.

content.text: Understand the concept of responsibility. Identify situations where responsibility is important.
Whiteboard, markers, Responsibility definition poster, Real-life scenario cards, Responsibility worksheet 1
Begin with a discussion about what the students think responsibility means.
Write down their ideas on the whiteboard.
Introduce the concept of responsibility and its importance in everyday life.
Distribute real-life scenario cards to small groups of students.
Each group discusses the scenario and identifies who is responsible for that situation.
Groups share their findings with the class.
Students complete the worksheet by matching responsibilities with appropriate scenarios.
Review the worksheet as a class.
Discuss the importance of being responsible and how it affects others.
2.1 Oral Communication: Going to the Shop………….pg # 20
Assign students to write a short paragraph about a time they demonstrated responsibility.
Instructions: Write the responsibilities that are given below with the correct pictures.
Planting and taking care of a garden
Draw a Picture of a Responsibility:
Now, draw a picture of a responsibility that you know but is not shown in the pictures above.
Objective: Identify themes of responsibility in literature, Write sentences about responsibility.
Skill focused on: Reading and Writing
Recap the previous day's lesson on responsibility.
Read a story from the storybook with a responsibility theme.
Discuss the responsibility themes and characters in the story.
Ask students to share their thoughts on what the characters could have done differently.
Provide sentence prompts related to responsibility on the whiteboard.
Each student writes sentences using the prompts.
Students share their sentences and discuss them as a class.
Students complete the worksheet by writing sentences about responsibility using given scenarios.
Assign students to read a short article or news story about a responsible action and write a summary.
Objective: Understand nouns, gender, modal verbs in grammar. Apply them to sentences.
Review the previous day's lesson on responsibility.
Introduce nouns, gender, and modal verbs.
Use grammar posters and examples to explain each concept.
Provide sentence construction cards with nouns, gender, and modal verbs.
Students form sentences using the cards and share them with the class.
Students complete the worksheet by filling in the blanks with the correct nouns, genders, or modal verbs.
Review the worksheet and discuss any challenging concepts.
Assign students to read a short article or news story about a responsible action and write a summary.
Day 4: Past Continuous Tense and Prepositions
Understand past continuous tense and prepositions. Apply them to sentences about responsibility.
Review the previous day's grammar concepts.
Introduce the past continuous tense and prepositions.
Use grammar posters and examples to explain each concept.
Provide sentence construction cards with past continuous tense and prepositions.
Students form sentences using the cards and share them with the class.
Students complete the worksheet by filling in the blanks with the correct past continuous tense verbs and prepositions.
Review the worksheet and discuss any challenging concepts.
Assign students to write a short story using past continuous tense and prepositions to describe responsible actions.
Day 5: Study Skills and Fun with Twins Poem
Develop dictionary skills, Enjoy and analyze a poem about responsibility.
Dictionary for each student, Textbook pg # 36 "Twins" poem, Responsibility worksheet 5, Whiteboard and markers
Review the previous day's grammar concepts and assignments.
Explain the importance of using a dictionary.
Show students how to look up words in a dictionary (e.g., alphabetical order, word meanings).
Practice by looking up a few words as a class.
Read the poem "Twins" aloud to the class.
Discuss the poem's meaning and themes related to responsibility.
Students use their dictionaries to find the meanings of words related to responsibility.
Review the worksheet and discuss the meanings of the words.
Assign students to write a short reflection on what they have learned about responsibility during the week.
Summarize the week's lessons on responsibility.
Encourage students to reflect on the importance of responsibility in their lives.
Part 1: Oral Communication - Going to the Shop(10 points)
Can the student explain the concept of responsibility in their own words? (5 points)
During the group discussion on real-life scenarios, did the student actively participate and contribute meaningful insights? (5 points)
After reading the story related to responsibility, can the student identify the main responsibility themes in the story? (5 points)
Did the student provide thoughtful responses when discussing what the characters in the story could have done differently to demonstrate responsibility? (5 points)
Can the student construct sentences effectively using proper grammar and vocabulary related to responsibility? (5 points)
Are the sentences written by the student clear and relevant to the topic of responsibility? (5 points)
Part 4: Grammar - Noun, Gender, Modal Verb, Past Continuous Tense, Prepositions (20 points)
Evaluate the student's understanding and usage of nouns, gender, modal verbs, past continuous tense, and prepositions in sentences related to responsibility. (20 points)
Part 5: Study Skills - Dictionary Skills (10 points)
Did the student effectively use a dictionary to find the meaning of a responsibility-related word? (5 points)
Is the student able to provide an accurate definition for the word found in the dictionary? (5 points)
Can the student identify and discuss responsibility themes in the "Twins" poem? (5 points)
Did the student actively participate in the discussion about the poem and contribute meaningful insights? (5 points)
Can the student provide a thoughtful reflection on what they have learned about responsibility during the week? (10 points)
What thing(s) will the students be able to do when this unit is complete?
What were the most effective elements of the lesson?
